item.title: ‘Cockroach Movement’ Forces Out India’s Education Minister
item.description: Indian Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday in response to rising pressure from student-led protests.

media:content.media:description: Supporters of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) celebrate following the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan on July 25, 2026 in New Delhi, India.

item.content:encoded:
Indian Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on Saturday amid mounting pressure from the “Cockroach Movement,” which demanded major government reforms—starting with his departure. Student activists accused Pradhan of failing to safeguard a competitive medical school exam, the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET), after authorities concluded that its contents had been leaked online.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) started as a parody account on social media after Indian authorities invalidated the annual medical school entry exam in May. Its name alludes to a comment made by Chief Justice Surya Kant during an unrelated hearing the same month, in which he compared young unemployed people to "cockroaches” and “parasites.”

However, the CJP quickly established itself as a formidable movement as anti-government sentiment erupted in the wake of the NEET scandal. The page gained millions of followers, and its founder began organizing protests in late June.  

Read More: What Is the Youth-Led ‘Cockroach Movement’ Staging Mass Protests in India?

How a Leaked Exam Sparked a National Movement

Over 2 million prospective students had taken the three-hour exam, according to the BBC. However, an exam coach noticed that a “guess paper”—or practice test—being circulated online seemed to closely match the exam itself, prompting an investigation. Police ultimately concluded that the questions had been leaked. They also discovered that some individuals paid as much as 5,000 rupees (about $52) to access the “guess paper” on WhatsApp, the Indian Express reported.

News that the exam results had been voided distressed many of the test-takers. The medical school system in India offered fewer than 130,000 slots for the undergraduate medical program this year, according to India’s National Medical Commission, making the selection process extremely competitive. The stakes are considerable, especially for those with limited financial resources. After the exam was discredited, at least 20 students died by suicide, according to Agence France-Presse. Protesters blamed the deaths on what they described as systemic failures in India's education system, and directed much of their anger toward Pradhan.

In a statement posted to social media after he stepped down, Pradhan said that the government would be switching to a computer-based testing model in the future to help prevent fraud and confirmed that a replacement exam had been successfully completed in June.

“India’s youth power is the real strength of this nation,” he wrote. 

Without accepting fault, he explained that he had agreed to step down in order to prevent “anti-national forces” from exploiting the upheaval. 

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP, celebrated the resignation with fellow protesters in New Delhi on Saturday.

“It's a victory for the people of India,” Dipke said to the crowd. He later posted an image of India’s Constitution on social media, with the caption: “Thank you.”

How the Protests Forced the Government to the Table

Despite police orders not to march on Parliament, tens of thousands of protesters attempted to do so last week and clashed with local authorities. The following day, they escalated their efforts by attempting to block public transportation, setting up barricades at the entrance of key metro stations and disrupting travel for millions of daily commuters. The police used tear gas and batons to disperse protesters, sparking public outrage. 

Activist Sonam Wangchuk was then forcibly taken to hospital after 26 days of a hunger strike meant to bring attention to protesters’ demands. He told local media outlets that he concluded his campaign after receiving assurances that the “issue of accountability” for the failures of the exam would be discussed by Parliament.

Upon hearing the news of the Education Minister’s resignation on Saturday, he told reporters that he welcomed the move.

"This is a victory for democracy that we witnessed today,” he said. “I congratulate and thank our CJP team who first raised this issue, as well as the volunteers who supported them, the students, youth, and elders from across the country who stood up for democracy.”

"I hope we maintain this peace and that no wrongdoing occurs anywhere in the future. We need to work on reforms. A nation isn't built by resignation alone," he added.

On the advice of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Indian President Droupadi Murmu appointed Pralhad Joshi—who already oversees the ministries of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, along with New and Renewable Energy—to oversee the Ministry of Education “in addition to his existing portfolio,” which is a typical arrangement in India following a Cabinet vacancy and does not preclude a later permanent appointment.

Joshi addressed the exam leak in May, saying, “The reforms are needed, we are bringing them, but they cannot be done within a year. By next year, technology-driven examination will be there."

CJP Spokesperson Saurav Das said in an interview with local media ANI following the president’s announcement that the party members will be meeting the new education minister “very soon.”

“Whoever becomes the Education Minister should know that the youth are watching. They will demand accountability,” Das said. “So, when the time comes, work in the interest of the youth. Stop paper leaks.”

What Comes Next for the CJP?

The CJP established its list of demands on May 16. In addition to calling for Pradhan’s resignation, the CJP asked for compensation of 10 million rupees ($104,000) for each student who died by suicide following the leak. 

They also sought greater legislative oversight of the educational system, gender equity in government roles, a fully independent media, and certain reforms to the electoral and political system—such as creating a 20-year ban on politicians switching parties before seeking election.

Adding to those mandates, the CJP last week asked that the central government drop any potential charges against protesters, after claiming that several had been “illegally detained” by police. 

Following Pradhan’s resignation, representatives from the CJP met with officials from the Indian government to discuss the rest of the party’s demands. In a press conference following the meeting, Das said on Saturday that the negotiations had been successful.

"All our demands have been accepted,” he said, without elaboration. “We request the protesters to withdraw immediately and return home peacefully."

The CJP added during the press conference on Saturday that representatives from the movement would meet with officials again in four weeks to work on broader reforms. Its spokesperson told local media that the fight for a transparent educational system is far from over. 

He said that members of the CJP conveyed to officials that if the issues are not addressed, the protesters will reconvene “and demand accountability.”

item.title: Understanding The Fraught Politics Of Powering AI
item.description: Growing anxiety over electricity bills, on the rise in part because of the AI-driven infrastructure buildout, has quickly become a liability for industry and politicians alike

media:content.media:credit: Photo by Saul Loeb / AFP via Getty Images
media:content.media:description: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during an event about the Ratepayer Protection Pledge at the Environmental Protection Agency in Washington D.C. on July 23

item.content:encoded:
Sitting at the Environmental Protection Agency with a mix of CEOs and cabinet officials, President Trump announced this week that a group of more than 200 stakeholders including governors, utility companies, and data center developers had signed up for his Ratepayer Protection Pledge, vowing to protect consumers from the rising costs of electricity.

The announcement is an attempt to hold off the growing anxiety over electricity bills, which are on the rise in part because of the AI-driven infrastructure buildout. The anxiety has quickly become a liability for industry and politicians alike.


But there’s also little doubt that the pledge, which is voluntary with no enforcement mechanism, is just tinkering around the edges of the issue. And the slower policymakers are to take decisive, substantive action, the more likely it becomes that today’s targeted fixes give way to demands for wholesale restructuring.

Two days before Trump launched his updated pledge, I moderated a panel at the Aspen Ideas Climate summit in Chicago addressing issues of rising electricity costs and reliability issues on the grid. The most interesting exchange came over the needed scale of solutions. 


Allison Clements, a former member of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, argued that states and utilities should move quickly to insulate customers from the cost of data centers, citing a range of regulatory tweaks. University of Chicago economist Michael Greenstone pushed back, suggesting that instead policymakers should use this moment to rethink the country’s fundamentally inefficient electricity system, reimagining how rates are designed to begin with and giving federal regulators greater authority to build transmission. “One should not waste a crisis,” he said.     

In today’s political environment, Greenstone’s call for bold thinking can seem a bit out of touch. Congress can barely keep the government open. It’s hard to imagine the body taking on the extremely complex and politically fraught job of reforming the country’s power system. And yet there is a case for thinking bigger—or at the very least laying the groundwork for bigger thinking. 


Right now, the affordability agenda is front of mind and elected officials are responding. In PJM, the Mid Atlantic part of the U.S. grid, officials have implemented a price cap when utilities bid for electricity, even as critics warn the move could discourage new investment. In Indiana, the governor removed the head of the state’s public utility commission after it approved a rate increase. Across the country the political incentive is to keep bills down today even if doing so complicates tomorrow’s reliability challenge. 

 

The system is holding together now. But it’s easy to imagine extreme weather—whether a catastrophic heat wave or deep winter freeze—creating more demand than the system can handle. If demand outstrips supply, rolling blackouts would create a new wave of political anger.     


“I can tell you with absolute certainty that if a grid operator has to choose on the hottest day of summer, whether to send power to a data center to run AI 24/7 or to a residential household that needs air conditioning, it's going to that data center,” says Neil Chatterjee, a former FERC commissioner. “And that's where the pitchforks come out.”


As alarming as pitchforks may be, they also create an opening for a big picture rethinking of how we produce and distribute electricity in the U.S. Indeed, major infrastructure reforms are more likely to happen because the status quo is intolerable than because someone diligently explained the benefits. 

With that in mind, a crisis could unlock much-touted but still elusive permitting reform that makes it easier to build energy infrastructure. It could make the case for a muscular FERC. And I’ve even heard the suggestion that the present moment creates an opportunity to revise the bedrock federal laws that have created challenges in this moment, including the Federal Power Act, the century-old law that governs interstate power transmission. 


The implications of such a move are dramatic. If done right, such reform could be a win for efforts to tackle climate change, given how much clean power has been hampered by a lack of transmission. (And climate advocates could end up being a powerful part of a reform coalition). It would also threaten the utility business model, long dependent on monopolies and state policy. It could be a boon for AI companies that want to move faster, though obviously not everyone would support that. 

A true crisis may be coming soon. It’s unclear who is ready to use it.

item.title: What Octogenarian Pop Divas Show Us About a Life Well-Lived
item.description: Cher, Dolly Parton, Barbra Streisand, and Dionne Warwick, all in their 80s, show us that conviction outlasts fashion, writes Debbie Millman.

media:content.media:credit: Stewart Cook—CBS/Getty Images; Jason Kempin—Getty Images; Kevin Mazur—BSB/Getty Images; Frank Hoensch—Redferns/Getty Images
media:content.media:description: Cher, Dolly Parton, Barbra Streisand, and Dionne Warwick

item.content:encoded:
On May 20, Cher turned 80 years old. Beyond a celebration of one spectacular career, her birthday is an occasion to consider what it means for a woman to maintain long-term relevance. It opens a larger question about endurance, public scrutiny, and what it takes to live a long, authentic life.

Cher, Dolly Parton, Barbra Streisand, and Dionne Warwick, all now in their 80s, were criticized for qualities that made them distinctive: being too country, too Jewish, too outspoken, too ambitious, too artificial, too stubborn. Rather than soften those edges, they built careers around them. The traits that once made them targets of ridicule eventually became their signatures.

In a culture that prizes constant reinvention, these octogenarian pop divas suggest another path: longevity through self-definition. They evolved, certainly, but without surrendering the core identities that made them recognizable in the first place. A life well-lived, they remind us, is not the life that pleased the most people, made the fewest demands, or aged into quiet respectability. A good life is one lived on its own terms, refusing every invitation to become smaller, softer, or less fully oneself.

Cher has spent more than six decades in the public eye, moving through music, television, film, fashion, tabloid culture, political commentary, heartbreak, reinvention, ridicule, camp, glamour, and triumph. She’s won a Grammy, an Emmy, an Academy Award, three Golden Globes, and is the only artist to have a number one single on a Billboard chart in seven consecutive decades.

She has been labeled too artificial, too outrageous, too sexual, too blunt, and too much. In the 1970s, her collaboration with Bob Mackie produced dresses that seemed designed to violate every rule of respectable female presentation: sheer, beaded, feathered, midriff-baring, unapologetically theatrical. In 1975, she appeared on the cover of TIME magazine in what was referred to as designer Bob Mackie’s “naked dress,”and in 1986, after being passed over for an Oscar nomination for the movie Mask despite winning Best Actress at Cannes, she arrived at the Academy Awards in a black Mackie ensemble with a towering feathered headdress, a bare midriff, and enough defiance to overwhelm the room. 

The criticism intensified when Cher refused to separate glamour from sexuality as she aged. In 1989, the video for “If I Could Turn Back Time,” filmed aboard the USS Missouri, placed her in a sheer black bodysuit, fishnets, leather jacket, and little else, performing for a cheering crowd of sailors. MTV initially banned the video and later aired it only after 9 p.m. The Navy, which had expected something more conservative, was reportedly embarrassed by the result. What the controversy revealed was not merely discomfort with a costume, but discomfort with a woman in her forties presenting herself as erotic, funny, commanding, and entirely in control of the spectacle.

Through all of it, she never seemed remotely interested in becoming more palatable. At one point in the late 1980s, her body was so scrutinized that there was a debate as to whether or not she had several ribs removed. (She didn’t.) Cher has acknowledged some cosmetic surgery, denied the more lurid inventions, refused the premise that her body required public adjudication, and defiantly stated, “If I want to put my tits on my back, it is nobody’s business but my own.” 

Cher’s dexterity shows up beyond how she survived being mocked for excess. It is revealed by how she transformed excess into architecture. Her costumes, wigs, cosmetic surgery, her public romances, the one-name fame: they constitute the visual and emotional vocabulary she has deftly controlled. Spectacle has never been a mask Cher has hid behind; it is the medium through which she insists on being seen.

This refusal has become Cher’s version of authorship. She has never disappeared into the trope expected of aging women. Instead, she made “too much” the unmistakable, driving force of her power.

Dolly Parton, also 80, spent years being deemed too country, too buxom, too rhinestoned, too blonde, too much of an exaggeration to be taken seriously. Late-night hosts and interviewers repeatedly treated her body as public property and her appearance as a punchline. Johnny Carson joked about her breasts on The Tonight Show; countless others followed the same overly trodden path. 

Parton’s genius was that rather than avoiding the joke, she took control of it. She understood, earlier than almost anyone, that being underestimated could become its own form of power. 

Long before she was appreciated as a national treasure, Parton knew who was really in control of the performance. When she joked that, “it costs a lot of money to look this cheap,” she playfully named the labor, money, intelligence, and craft inside the caricature. Her blonde hair, acrylic nails, high heels, rhinestones, waist-cinching silhouettes, and curves were not accidents of taste. They were the materials of a persona she built deliberately, then protected ferociously. 

Parton turned exaggeration into authorship through repetition and scale. On album covers like Jolene, she presented mountain-girl glamour as a code. In the film 9 to 5, she transformed the image of the underestimated secretary into a working woman with wit, strategy, and rage. At Dollywood, which opened under her name in 1986 near the Tennessee mountains where she was raised, she converted her story into infrastructure: a theme park, a regional employer, a monument to Appalachian storytelling, craft, music, and belonging. What might have been dismissed as kitsch became an economic and cultural engine, directly employing approximately 4,000 people, creating more than 23,000 jobs in the region, and contributing $1.8 billion in annual economic impact to Tennessee.

In the process, Parton became one of the most accomplished songwriters, performers, philanthropists, and entrepreneurs in the world. She has written thousands of songs, including “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “9 to 5,” and “I Will Always Love You,” the latter becoming a rare song that defined two different eras through two different women’s voices. Parton has been inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, the Country Music Hall of Fame, the Songwriters Hall of Fame, and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Her Imagination Library, founded in 1995 in honor of her father, who never learned to read or write, has now gifted more than 300 million books to children. The program began in her home county in Tennessee and has grown across multiple countries. 

What makes Parton’s endurance so instructive is that she never abandoned the mountain-girl mythology from which she first emerged. She expanded it. She made it capacious enough to hold country music, film, children’s literacy, vaccine philanthropy, theme parks, baking mixes, fashion, and business. The rhinestones were never a distraction from the seriousness of her work. They were part of the strategy.

The starmaker machinery has long depended on a narrow definition of beauty and controlling the behavior of women. Barbra Streisand, now 84, was told early and often that the things that made her unmistakable were liabilities. She was too Jewish, too nasal, too Brooklyn, too ambitious, too controlling, too unwilling to be remade into someone else’s idea of a star.  

From the start of her career, people told her to fix her nose. In 1964, even this magazine reported as much. In her memoir, she recalls being told by several people that she should get a nose job and have her teeth capped. But she feared that changing her nose might change her voice, and refused, certain that her talent should be enough. 

It was enough, but not before the culture made her pay for it. When Streisand fought to make Yentl, the 1983 film she co-wrote, produced, directed, and starred in, she spent years trying to persuade Hollywood that she could direct it. The film itself is about a Jewish woman who refuses the limits imposed on her mind and disguises herself as a man in order to study, and the parallel was impossible to miss. 

For that insistence, she was often described as “difficult,” a word that frequently means a woman has declined to pretend she has no standards. Streisand has spoken directly about that double standard: a man who asks for a shot to be changed is treated as committed; a woman who asks for the same thing is treated as obsessive. But the very qualities that made her controversial—precision, control, refusal, an almost forensic relationship to detail—also made her work possible.

Dionne Warwick, now 85, offers yet another version of endurance on her own terms. She has been criticized as too direct for those who prefer female softness, too dry for those who mistake composure for distance, and, at various points, judged through racial expectations that flattened the sophistication of her achievement. In 1963, the European record cover featured a white model on the cover of her album, An Empty Place. Her crossover success with Burt Bacharach and Hal David brought her an enormous white audience, but it also exposed her to criticism that her sound was too polished, too restrained, and not sufficiently aligned with what some listeners expected from a Black female singer. 

Warwick’s first hit already contained a declaration of self-possession. In 1962, after learning that “Make It Easy on Yourself,” a song she had hoped would become her first single, had been given to Jerry Butler, she snapped at Bacharach and David, “Don’t make me over.” They turned the phrase into a song. It became Warwick’s first solo hit and, in retrospect, a thesis statement.

Her power has always resided in composure. In songs like “Walk On By,” “Anyone Who Had a Heart,” “I Say a Little Prayer,” and “A House Is Not a Home,” Warwick sang with elegance, intelligence, and restraint. “Walk On By,” released in 1964, is a devastating song precisely because she refuses to overperform devastation. The lyric asks an old lover to keep walking if they see her breaking down; Warwick sings it as though dignity itself is the last remaining shelter. In her performances, she commanded the room by withholding exactly enough.

In recent years, Warwick has also become beloved by younger generations for the directness that has defined her public persona. On Twitter (now X) she began asking questions with the kind of plainspoken authority that felt almost radical in a culture addicted to irony. Why, she asked Chance the Rapper, did he need to include “the Rapper” in his name if he was very obviously a rapper? She wondered publicly about The Weeknd’s spelling. The exchange with Chance the Rapper eventually led to a collaboration, but the larger revelation was that Warwick had not become newly direct. New audiences had simply discovered the clarity that had always been there.

She does not appear to be chasing relevance so much as allowing new audiences to catch up. That distinction matters: there is a difference between remaining visible because one is desperate to be relevant and remaining visible because one is confident in their own skin. Warwick’s authority comes from that confidence.

None of these superstars survived and thrived by becoming less themselves, and this is what makes their continued cultural relevance so instructive. They teach us that to age successfully and gracefully, we need not reinvent ourselves, but rather to know who we are and to evolve.  

Make no mistake; these octogenarians have certainly evolved. Cher moved from folk-pop duo to television star to Oscar-winning actress to dance-floor futurist to Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductee and memoirist. Parton moved from the Porter Wagoner Show to pop crossover to film to Dollywood to global philanthropy. Streisand moved from nightclub singer to Broadway phenomenon to film star to director, producer, and author. Warwick moved from the Scepter Records years to global pop elegance to activist, survivor, internet oracle, and elder stateswoman of direct address.

But for each of these women, adapting to new stages and industries has been conducted on their own terms, without compromising the essence of who they have always been. Their careers were built on deepening their commitments to themselves until the very qualities once deemed excessive became iconic.

Women are often instructed to age by diminishing. They are instructed, both explicitly and implicitly, to gracefully accept less attention, less power, less sexuality, less ambition, and less contradiction. They are praised for aging gracefully (which usually means aging quietly and out of sight). They are expected to become wiser but not louder, visible but not vain, accomplished but not demanding, and well-preserved but not provocative. Even admiration can become a form of containment, turning older women into monuments rather than allowing them to be monumental. 

Cher, Parton, Streisand, and Warwick have resisted these strictures. They have not aged into neutrality. Pop divas in their 80s show us that conviction outlasts fashion. They made new work, took risks, changed formats, survived failures, and were undeterred. They did so without compromising the traits that made them singular. 

At a moment when many people feel pressured to change themselves to meet the expectations of others, these octogenarian icons offer a different model of a life well-lived: one built not on perpetual reinvention, but on the courage to remain unmistakably oneself.

A life well-lived, they remind us, is not the life that pleased the most people, made the fewest demands, or aged into quiet respectability. A good life is one lived on its own terms, refusing every invitation to become smaller, softer, or less fully oneself.

item.title: What Is Pickaxe Mountain, Iran’s Underground Nuclear Site That Trump Is Threatening?
item.description: An expert tells TIME why the underground facility is at the center of much debate.

media:content.media:description: Vantor satellite image shows an overview of Natanz nuclear site and adjacent Pickaxe Mountain mining area in Isfahan Province, Iran, on Nov. 14, 2025.

item.content:encoded:
As the resumption of the Iran war escalates, with Washington and Tehran trading a deluge of strikes, President Donald Trump has again threatened to attack sites linked to Iran’s nuclear programme.

In the Oval Office on Tuesday, Trump was asked if he believes Iran has moved nuclear centrifuges into Pickaxe Mountain, an underground site near one of the country's primary enrichment facilities.

“They may have, we don’t have it on record,” Trump said. “It doesn’t mean anything unless they have the material [uranium]. We follow the material, that’s where the action is.”

“We’ll be hitting that area, probably pretty soon, and there’s not a thing they can do about it,” he added, having earlier vowed that “any site where they’re even thinking about nuclear, we’ll be hitting it very powerfully."

This is far from the first time Trump has threatened to strike Pickaxe Mountain, known in Iran as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La.

The resumption of the Iran war on July 7, just weeks after the signing of the interim cease-fire agreement, has largely focused on the continued struggle over the Strait of Hormuz. But the other long-standing prevalent issue surrounds Iran’s nuclear capabilities, as Trump has repeatedly stated that Tehran must never be allowed to build or procure a nuclear weapon.

“We're going to take out Pickaxe Mountain. Tell the Iranians to be ready,” Trump said in a July 13 interview, once again bringing focus to the nuclear-linked site.

Amid the escalating threats and tensions, here’s what to know about the Iranian facility.

What is Pickaxe Mountain?

The underground site is situated around 220 km (140 ‌miles) south of Tehran and 2 km (1.2 miles) from the Natanz nuclear complex.

In June last year, the U.S. joined Israel in launching strikes on three key Iranian nuclear sites—an action Trump said had “completely and totally obliterated” the targeted facilities.

Natanz was among the facilities hit, as it was believed to house highly-enriched uranium. The entrances to the nuclear site were targeted again in the early days of the Iran war which started on Feb. 28.

During last year's 12-day war, the nuclear facility outside the city of Isfahan, about 80 miles away, was also bombed. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has said tunnels at that facility is likely where a cache of some 970 pounds of enriched uranium are being stored.

According to the U.S.-based Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS), the tunnel facility under construction at Pickaxe Mountain has not been previously targeted in either June 2025 or the 2026 war, “aside from the destruction of a vehicle on a nearby spoil pile, which we believe was most likely associated with air defense.”

Construction of the Pickaxe Mountain facility started in 2020, after a fire at Natanz, which Iran's nuclear body argued had been caused by an act of sabotage.

Iran at the time said the underground halls were intended to replace the destroyed above-ground advanced centrifuge assembly facility at the Natanz site, according to ISIS.

“It's a very deep facility. We don't know exactly how deep, but it's very likely at least 100 meters deep,” James Acton, co-director of the Nuclear Policy Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, tells TIME.

The highly-fortified site would be a difficult target for the U.S., experts say.

“There's just no way to destroy this facility. The best one can do is try to collapse the tunnel entrances," explains Acton.

Is Pickaxe Mountain a functioning site?

Trump said earlier this month that the U.S. is watching Pickaxe Mountain “closely" and doesn't see any activity there.

ISIS’ assessment, based on satellite imagery, is that the facility is not yet operational, but construction continues.

The think tank said it “remains unclear when Pickaxe Mountain could be operational… It is also unclear if Iran still plans on installing a large-scale assembly facility, given the destruction of Iran’s centrifuge program, including Iran’s ability to make centrifuge components needed for an assembly plant.”

Esmail Baghaei, spokesperson for the Iranian Foreign Ministry, has said there is no nuclear action at the site, insisting any of Iran’s nuclear activities have “been fully declared to the IAEA, in accordance with its safeguards obligations.”

“Washington’s obsessive focus on Kolang Kouh, where no nuclear activity is taking place, is nothing more than a fabricated pretext for aggression, destruction, and sabotage,” he said on July 22.

If Iran starts to rebuild its centrifuge manufacturing capability, “it could plan to install a smaller centrifuge assembly facility in Pickaxe Mountain able to serve a nuclear weapons program,” according to ISIS.

Acton tells TIME it remains a "legitimate concern” that Pickaxe Mountain could potentially be used for “more than just secure storage.”

“The concern is, whether or not it was developed as an enrichment plant, the fear is now that it would be used as one,” he says.

Rafael Grossi, chief of the United Nations’ nuclear watchdog IAEA, told PBS in March that Iran had previously “announced its intention to have nuclear activity” at Pickaxe Mountain, referring to it as “part of their quite systematic intention to put their most sensitive facilities underground.”

Grossi said the IAEA inspectors had not been granted access to the Pickaxe Mountain site.

Additionally, the nuclear watchdog has been unable to independently verify Iran’s centrifuge capacity and production since 2021, so Tehran may have reserves despite strikes over the last two years.

With the destruction of Iran’s other centrifuge related facilities, “the Pickaxe Mountain complex is a potential candidate site for any Iranian reconstitution of its centrifuge program, from centrifuge component production to centrifuge assembly to uranium enrichment,” ISIS stated in November 2025.

Trump's nuclear row with Iran

Shortly before the U.S. military conducted its 13th consecutive evening of strikes against Iran on Thursday, Trump again accused Tehran of having “evil intentions” and insisted “we cannot let them, ever, even think about having a nuclear weapon.”

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei in April vowed to protect its nuclear and missile capabilities in direct defiance of Trump. He said his country will defend its “fundamental and modern technologies—from nano and bio to nuclear and missile—as their national capital and will guard them like their maritime, land, and air borders.”

Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is “peaceful,” but concerns remain among Western leaders.

The Memorandum of Understanding signed on June 17 asserts that Iran can never develop a nuclear weapon—a promise the regime has made in the past. The agreement states that the U.S. and Iran will address Iran’s existing stockpile of enriched material, “with the minimum methodology to be down blending on site” under the supervision of inspectors with the IAEA.

It also said both countries had “acknowledged the critical importance of the nuclear issues… and expressed their intention to immediately address these issues in the negotiations in order to achieve mutual agreement on them.”

The interim agreement laid out the terms of an extended 60-day cease-fire to allow time for technical talks to take place. That deadline is set to expire in mid-August, but the resumption of the war has brought the entire deal into question.

item.title: Trump Will Give ‘Unifying Yet Vicious’ Speech at Rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Dinner, White House Says
item.description: After the shooting at the April event, Trump revealed that he had intended to rip into the media during his speech, but would now likely not do so.

media:content.media:description: President Donald Trump speaks at Wheeler High School in Marietta, Georgia, on July 22, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump will be giving a “unifying yet vicious” speech at the rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Dinner on Friday evening, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt previewed.

“The President’s speech will be a combination of unifying yet vicious, and serious yet hilarious, all at the same time, if you can imagine that,” Leavitt told NBC News. “One thing I can assure you, it will be entertaining.”

Last month, the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) announced that it was rescheduling its annual dinner to July 24, after its event in April was disrupted by a gunman who charged a security checkpoint at the venue and exchanged fire with law enforcement before he was apprehended.

“The White House Correspondents’ Dinner has served as a celebration of a free press and the vital role of journalism in our democracy for over a century,” WHCA President Weijia Jiang said in a letter to association members last month. “When gunfire interrupted this year’s event, it further clarified the WHCA’s mission to advocate for the freedoms that are protected in the First Amendment.”

“We will not allow an act of violence to have the last word,” she continued.

Jiang said at the time that the July dinner “will feature significantly enhanced safety measures and new access procedures,” and that the event “will be a more intimate gathering.”

The WHCA also announced earlier this week that it will present an award to Secret Service Police Officer Victor Gonzales, who the Secret Service said "heroically engaged the armed suspect, placing himself directly in harm's way” and ended up being “struck in his protective vest.”

“Officer Gonzales played a significant role when he ran toward danger so that thousands of others could make it home safely,” Jiang said in a statement. “His courage stemmed from a dedication to service, which we are looking forward to honoring this week.”

The WHCA said that it would also award the staff of the Washington Hilton, the venue for the April dinner, with the same special recognition at the rescheduled event.

“Even after the men and women of the Washington Hilton experienced a harrowing situation, they continued to take care of guests,” Jiang said. “The WHCA appreciates their professionalism and commitment to service, which was on full display on April 25th. Every member of the team deserves to be recognized for their dedication.”

Trump applauded the WHCA last month for rescheduling the event, calling it “a sign of Strength and Fortitude,” and added that he had once again been invited to speak. The April dinner that was interrupted by gunfire was the first time that Trump, who has had a contentious relationship with the press, had attended the Correspondents’ Dinner as President.

After the shooting in April, Trump revealed that he had initially intended to rip into the media during his speech at the event, but that he would likely not do so now.

“I don’t know if I could ever be as rough as I was going to be tonight,” he said after the Washington Hilton was evacuated the night of the shooting. “I think I’m going to be probably very nice. I’ll be very boring the next time, but we’re going to have a great event.”

After the WHCA announced the rescheduled dinner in June, Trump again suggested that his speech may not be as harsh as the one he planned to deliver in April.

“I don’t know whether or not I will give the same rather nasty statements, at least as it concerns certain people, but we will soon find out,” he said on Truth Social. “In any event, it will be a ‘HOT’ ticket!”

item.title: How to Know If You’re Eligible for a Piece of the $2.5 Billion Amazon Prime Settlement, and How to File a Claim
item.description: The deadline to submit a claim for compensation under the historic settlement is fast approaching.

media:content.media:description: Low-angle view of the side of a blue trailer semi truck with the logo for Amazon Prime in San Ramon, California, on October 8, 2018.

item.content:encoded:
The deadline is fast approaching for eligible Amazon Prime subscribers to file a claim to receive a portion of a historic $2.5 billion settlement the company reached with the Federal Trade Commission.

Amazon agreed to the deal last September to settle a lawsuit over allegations that “millions of customers into “unknowingly” enrolling in its paid Amazon Prime service and then made the subscriptions difficult to cancel. 

The settlement requires Amazon to stop those alleged practices and pay heft fines—as well as offering “full relief for the estimated 35 million consumers impacted by unwanted Prime enrollment or deferred cancellation.”

Amazon has denied any wrong-doing. 

"Amazon and our executives have always followed the law and this settlement allows us to move forward and focus on innovating for customers,” the company said in a statement following the settlement announcement. “We work incredibly hard to make it clear and simple for customers to both sign up or cancel their Prime membership, and to offer substantial value for our many millions of loyal Prime members around the world.”

The deadline for submitting a claim for compensation under the settlement is July 27.

Here’s how to know if you’re eligible for a portion of the settlement, and how to file a claim. 

Who's eligible?

To be eligible for a refund under the settlement, you must be an AmazonPrime customer in the U.S. who “unintentionally” signed up for the service through a “challenged enrollment flow” or attempted to cancel your subscription but were unable to between June 23, 2019, and June 23, 2025. 

According to the FTC, the challenged enrollment flows include the universal Amazon Prime decision page, shipping selection page, single page checkout, and the Prime Video enrollment flow. The agency noted that customers do not have to determine for themselves whether they signed up for Prime through one of those flows; Amazon will make that determination.

You are also only eligible for the settlement if you have used no more than three of Prime’s benefits, such as Prime Video or Prime Music, within any 12-month period after you enrolled in the service.

How to submit a claim

Eligible Amazon customers should have received a notice to file their claim by email or mail, according to the settlement website. 

Using a “Claim ID and PIN” included in the notice they received, customers can also access their claim form via the settlement website. There is also an option to file a claim through the website without those details contained in the notice. 

The claim form asks customers to provide their name, current address, and zip code, and to specify whether they were "unintentionally enrolled” in Prime or were unable to cancel during the designated time period. 

No documents are required to answer those questions, nor to prove whether you used Prime benefits during a 12-month period. 

Unlike private settlements, customers do not have the option to opt-out of government settlements like this one. 

The website advises customers to contact admin@SubscriptionMembershipSettlement.com for further support. 

How much compensation will claimants receive?

Eligible Prime customers will get a refund of their Prime fees, up to a maximum of $51.

Amazon expects to send out payments in late 2026.

item.title: How the World Is Reacting to Trump's 'Forced Labor' Tariffs
item.description: Officials around the world are pushing back on the rationale for the new import duties.

media:content.media:description: Canadian geese swim in front of the Port of Vancouver in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada, on Wednesday, July 22, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Officials around the world are pushing back on the claims of “forced labor” the Trump Administration has cited to impose sweeping new tariffs on over 80 countries.

The import duties, which will affect 60 economies and take effect on Friday, represent President Donald Trump’s latest effort to impose alternative tariffs on goods coming into the U.S. after the Supreme Court earlier this year struck down most of those he had put in place.

In a Thursday announcement, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) said the new tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% were being levied against dozens of countries “for their failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor.”

Read More: Trump’s New Tariffs on Over 80 Countries, Explained

“The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it’s well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement. “Today’s action will begin to correct what is both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice to improve the welfare of workers everywhere.”

The U.S. Tariff Act of 1930 prohibits importing goods whose production involved forced labor. Trump imposed the tariffs under Section 301 of the law, which allows for sanctions on countries that have engaged in trade practices that are “unreasonable or discriminatory and burdens or restricts United States commerce.”

Among the expansive group of countries that will be affected by the new tariffs are some of the U.S.’s closest allies and most major trading partners. Collectively, they account for roughly 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to a USTR factsheet.

Officials from a number of the impacted nations objected to the stated rationale for the tariffs, expressing a mix of disappointment, anger, and confusion.

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon called the 12.5% tariffs on his country  “extremely disappointing.”

“The US investigation did not provide meaningful evidence to support claims in relation to forced labour,” Luxon wrote on X. “Tariffs are not the way - they drive up costs and uncertainty for businesses.”

Australian Trade Minister Don Farrell likewise called the tariffs “completely unjustified” and vowed, while speaking to reporters, to continue pushing for the removal of “all tariffs on Australian goods.”

Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara also protested the tariffs.

“It is regrettable that the measure imposes tariffs on the grounds of non-existence of measures banning imports of goods made by forced labor, even though Japan’s industry and trade are in line with international rules,” Kihara said at a press conference.

China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs reiterated its stance that it “opposes all forms of unilateral tariffs.”

“Tariff wars and trade wars do not serve any parties’ interests,” ministry spokesman Lin Jian said at a press conference.

Norway’s Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide said "We are firmly opposed to the United States's unilateral use of customs duties against Norway and other countries.”

Brazil, striking the same chord, said that the tariffs were “arbitrary” and “unjustified.”

"Lacking a legal basis under domestic law to support its protectionist ​trade policy, the U.S. Trade Representative chose ​to manipulate an issue of great importance to ⁠human rights and workers' rights movement," the Brazilian government said in a statement. 

The majority of the affected countries were assigned a 12.5% rate for the new tariffs.

However, imports will be taxed at a slightly lower 10% rate for a group of 17 economies that the USTR in its fact sheet described as having “made commitments to adopt, and effectively enforce, forced labor import prohibitions.” Within that group of countries are Canada, India, Mexico, and the U.K., among others.

Officials from several of those countries offered more muted responses to the new levies, though they continued to note their opposition to Trump’s aggressive tariff approach.

Canadian Minister of Internal Trade Dominic LeBlanc, whose country Trump also hit with a separate 50% tariff hike earlier in the week, said the tariffs were “not unexpected,” since they came just as a 10% global tariff Trump previously imposed expired.

“Canada shares the United States’ objective of ensuring goods produced with forced labour do not enter our supply chains,” LeBlanc in a statement. 

He went on to stress, though, that “Canada has one of the world’s most robust frameworks to prevent and address forced labour, backed by strong legislative and enforcement measures.”

Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard similarly noted the timing of the new tariffs coinciding with the expiration of the others.

"One replaces the other, ​so tariff treatment is maintained,” Mexico's Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said on social media. 

Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin told BFM Business TV that Europe would likely see little change with the imposition of the new tariffs due to an agreement reached in July 2025 that set a cap on U.S. tariffs for most European Union goods at 15%.

"For Europe, it ought not to change much because we have the Turnberry agreement which should be ​respected by Donald Trump,” Moulin said. 

“But,” he added, “obviously it creates more uncertainty for world trade and clearly it's not favourable for growth.”

The British government also said that the new tariffs would have "no negative change" on its export economy. 

Other countries receiving the 10% tariff such as Malaysia, Cambodia, and Bangladesh stated that they were relieved or even pleased by the rate.

item.title: What Is Joe Manchin’s New Independent Leadership Council?
item.description: The council presents itself on its website as “an opportunity to fix politics.”

media:content.media:description: Then-Sen. Joe Manchin (I-WV) speaks to reporters outside the Senate Chamber on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on June 3, 2024.

item.content:encoded:
Former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin is embarking on a new initiative: a project called the Independent Leadership Council.

The council—which the 78-year-old former senator is running with his daughter, Heather Manchin—will recruit and support independent candidates who are launching congressional bids. The former Senator launched the initiative at an event on Thursday, with several candidates in attendance, including California Rep. Kevin Kiley, who previously identified as a Republican but is now running a reelection campaign as an independent.

“We’re not trying to start another party,” Manchin told CNN in an interview that was published on Friday. “We’re trying to get a person who can be committed to—and totally committed to—being an independent with an independent voice. They can vote with Democrats and Republicans when they’re right and speak out against them when they’re wrong.”

The Manchins told CNN that if the council decides to support candidates, it will help them with campaigning, fundraising, and on-the-ground organizing. The Manchins were optimistic that, if their support can help a candidate win in the November midterms, then they might be able to have an impact on the 2028 presidential race.

“Our hope is that this is kind of our pilot, experiment, trying to prove it can be done,” Heather Manchin told CNN.

The council presents itself on its website as “an opportunity to fix politics.”

“America was founded on the belief that freedom and competition make us stronger. Somewhere along the way, our politics lost sight of those principles,” the website reads. “Decades of partisanship carved a divide most Americans never wanted. Instead of choosing sides, we’re changing the game by charting a new path that gives leaders the freedom to serve people, not parties.”

Manchin served in the Senate for more than a decade. For most of his political career, he was a centrist member of the Democratic Party. But he dropped that affiliation in 2024, shortly before the end of his time in the upper chamber, and re-registered as an independent. Even before he left the party, he frequently broke from his Democratic colleagues in his votes on various issues, including on climate change and tax hikes on the wealthy. He repeatedly criticized the Democratic Party, arguing that there wasn’t space for more conservative Democrats like him.

“Since becoming a United States senator in 2010, I have seen both the Democrat and Republican parties leave West Virginia and our country behind for partisan extremism while jeopardizing our democracy,” he said in a statement when he announced that he was switching his political affiliation. “Today, our national politics are broken and neither party is willing to compromise to find common ground. To stay true to myself and remain committed to put country before party, I have decided to register as an independent with no party affiliation and continue to fight for America’s sensible majority.”

Manchin’s renewed pushback against partisan politics now comes at a time when majorities of American adults “have an unfavorable view” of the Republican Party and Democratic Party, according to a Gallup poll released in May. And a record-high 45% of Americans identified as independents last year, Gallup polling released in January found.

item.title: How OpenAI Lost Control of an AI Model—and What Needs to Change
item.description: TIME spoke with experts and insiders about what must change to prevent the next AI escape.

media:content.media:description: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman talks to reporters at the Dirksen Senate Office building in Washington, DC on June 3, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
OpenAI was evaluating its artificial intelligence models’ ability to exploit vulnerable software when instead the models hacked the infrastructure surrounding the test, broke containment, and attacked a real company, OpenAI revealed on July 21. Observers say this is the first real-world instance of AI doing something researchers have long worried about: a loss-of-control scenario. If the industry fails to learn from it, it is unlikely to be the last.

Hugging Face, a company that hosts AI models and datasets, was the target of the autonomous attack, and reported the incident to local police before it knew OpenAI’s models were responsible. The breach was serious, but the immediate consequences were limited. Had similar behavior occurred inside a hospital, power grid, or other critical system, it could have been much worse. 

Many have called the incident a “warning shot.” TIME spoke with experts and insiders about what it would take to heed that warning before a similar failure produces consequences that are harder to contain.

What happened?

On July 16, Hugging Face said it had been hit by an unusually automated cyberattack. Over the course of a weekend, AI agents carried out thousands of actions across many temporary virtual computers, moving through the company’s internal systems and shifting the infrastructure coordinating the attack between online services to keep it running. Five days later, OpenAI disclosed that its own models were responsible.

The models were trying to cheat on a cybersecurity test. OpenAI had placed them inside what it called a “highly isolated environment,” with only limited access to an internal service used to download approved software. They found a previously unknown flaw in that service, used it to break into other OpenAI systems and eventually reached the open internet. From there, they inferred that Hugging Face might hold material related to the test, broke into its systems and obtained information that helped them score higher.

“If a model of this capability level cannot be contained, what should we expect for future, much more powerful models? This is an important wake-up call both for risks from loss of control of powerful AI systems as well as organizational security for frontier labs,” says Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which tests AI models for deception and scheming.

Requiring disclosures before incidents become catastrophic

How long were the agents running? Did they work in unison? What was the prompt? These details remain unknown, at least to the public. Several experts TIME spoke with stressed that the lack of details make the severity of the incident hard to judge. 

OpenAI did not respond to TIME’s request for comment, but has said it has partnered with Hugging Face to conduct a thorough investigation and will share more details once complete. But perhaps more worryingly, OpenAI is not legally compelled to disclose the incident in the first place. 

California’s SB 53 and New York’s RAISE Act are recently passed state-level laws that require large AI companies to disclose critical safety incidents, but only if an incident risks causing more than 50 deaths or serious injuries, or more than $1 billion in property damage. “They have made the bar so high for anything to qualify, only the most grievous incidents will actually be reported,” says Mackenzie Arnold, director of U.S. policy at LawAI, an independent think tank focused on the legal challenges posed by artificial intelligence.

“The version of the RAISE Act that the NY Legislature passed would have required disclosure of this ‘incident.’ After lobbying from OpenAI, Bloomberg, and a16z, the final version the Governor signed allows companies to hide events like this,” Alex Bores, New York state representative and the bill’s sponsor posted to X. “I'm glad OpenAI chose to disclose this crime. The law shouldn't give them a choice,” he wrote.

Stronger containment

If AI can slip out of its box, you need a stronger box.

“Externally, this feels like a big warning shot, but internally, related incidents have been happening for a while,” says an OpenAI staffer, who spoke under the condition of anonymity. The day before OpenAI disclosed the incident, the company revealed that it had shut down another internal deployment after it realized it had slipped out of its sandbox—a digitally, rather than physically, separated environment. “Models have broken out of sandboxes before, and we always try to patch them,” the staffer says. “But the problem is … it's impossible to patch every single thing that a creative AI can do.”

The problem is not unique to OpenAI. Anthropic disclosed in April that it realized an internal deployment of Mythos had gained unauthorized access after one of its researchers received an email from the model while having lunch in a park.

As models surpass human ability to craft escape routes, the challenge of containment becomes daunting. “I think we do need to do that, but I think we also need to be prepared for a world where even best practices aren't really good enough,” says Peter Wildeford, head of policy at the AI Policy Network, a nonprofit that advocates for policies to help America prepare for a world where AI matches human cognition.

But while in theory, a superhuman AI system might outmaneuver even the most secure containers, there are also actions AI companies could take right now to improve security. Currently, there are no laws governing the security of internal deployments.

“Sandboxes are actually notoriously insecure,” says Heidy Khlaaf, chief AI scientist at AI Now Institute, and a former safety systems engineer contractor at OpenAI. The fact that the models were permitted to connect to a service for downloading packages meant the environment was not truly sealed off, she adds.

In a previous role, Khlaaf audited security at dozens of technology companies. Before that, she worked auditing high-risk systems, like those used inside nuclear power plants—which often “air gap” systems, physically cutting them from internet access. “What we consider safe in a nuclear plant is so different from what big tech considers safe.”

Catching mischievous agents in real time

The Hugging Face incident reveals the importance of real-time monitoring.

Though details of the precise timeline are scant, Hugging Face has said the agents worked over a “weekend,” suggesting that they were able to break containment and get up to no good for an extended period before OpenAI noticed and intervened. Actions carried out internally by agents on OpenAI’s Codex platform are carefully monitored, the OpenAI staffer says, but models undergoing evaluation are deployed on a separate system that is not monitored by default. 

Zack Korman, CEO of Oslo-based agent-oversight startup Embroidery, says real-time agent monitoring—even outside top AI companies—is commonplace, and to not carefully oversee a cybersecurity evaluation is “irresponsible.” You should be confident models cannot break free, “but also have monitoring just in case you're wrong,” he says.

OpenAI has said “this incident points to the need to further strengthen our model’s alignment, cyber protections during evaluation time, and monitoring during internal testing.”

Steering development towards safer AI systems

To prevent models from taking actions, OpenAI typically installs guardrails on its models after training to reduce the chance they’ll engage in harmful actions. In this instance, those cyber guardrails were disabled to properly measure its performance.

But the ultimate aim of the field of “AI alignment” is to ensure that such guardrails become less necessary as AI models naturally behave as intended. This is seen as particularly important to those who believe AI may become smart enough to route around guardrails.

“We train the models to be really good at accomplishing tasks and doing whatever it takes to accomplish those tasks,” the OpenAI staffer says. What remains an open technical question is how to guarantee those models don’t take unintentional or dangerous actions. “We're still nowhere near solving this misalignment problem,” they add. 

There’s another way the industry could steer development in a safer direction, Khlaaf says. While some abilities, like spotting vulnerabilities in software, are useful to attackers and defenders, designing exploits for those vulnerabilities uniquely empowers attackers. Khlaaf says that labs should put more resources into capabilities that directly help defenders, such as detecting attacks, writing secure code, and patching vulnerabilities. AI companies are already investing in some of those tasks, but their most visible capability gains and benchmarks have centered on finding vulnerabilities and constructing exploits, she says.

In an industry defined by speed, OpenAI has said the stricter infrastructure controls it has implemented in response have already slowed its “research velocity.” Hobbhahn says that’s a price worth paying. “This is humanity’s last technology. We cannot screw this up. So we need to err on the side of getting it right rather than getting it immediately.”

item.title: Christopher Nolan on Helen, Athena, and His New Ending for The Odyssey
item.description: The director discusses Zendaya and Lupita Nyong'o's characters

media:content.media:description: Christopher Nolan in Los Angeles on April 17, 2026

item.content:encoded:
This spring, I was among the first journalists to speak with Christopher Nolan about his highly anticipated adaptation of The Odyssey. Now, the movie is out and has become Nolan’s biggest worldwide opening ever.

In our initial interview, Nolan was reluctant to discuss the ending of The Odyssey. He’s known as the master of the last-act twist, and likes leaving the audience with more questions than answers. He told me he never wants to impose his interpretation on others. (Are Cobbs’ kids in Inception real or imagined? You decide.) But when I hopped on the phone again shortly before the film’s release to have a spoiler-filled chat about the film’s final act—readers beware!—he offered some insight as to why he made certain changes when adapting the epic poem.

We discussed the surprising parallels between The Odyssey and Oppenheimer, why Nolan decided to give Odysseus and Penelope the happy ending they don’t get in Homer’s epic poem, and how to interpret Zendaya’s mysterious character: Is she actually a goddess or merely a manifestation of Odysseus’ guilt? We also dug into Zeus’ Law and the deeper meaning behind Helen’s scarred face. 

TIME: Odysseus is a man who suffers from PTSD, and, in your interpretation, who believes he’s responsible for the end of a civilization because he violated the ethical code by which the ancient Greeks lived their lives.

Nolan: My form of storytelling is, you take a hero, as we did with Oppenheimer, and Oppenheimer has all these flaws, all of these complexities. You find an actor who can take the audience on a journey with that character and make mistakes with that character and not judge that character. And then you step back from that character and go, “Well, how did we get here?” 

[For this movie,] you do that through Odysseus’ men. That’s one of the things in the poem that’s breezed over—the way in which the crew ends up getting killed one by one, despite his leadership. In the process of adaptation, you go, “That’s actually pretty interesting. Maybe we need to make that more center stage.” What’s the relationship between him and his crew? How do they feel about how he’s leading them and the things that befall them?

He’s a guy who makes a lot of mistakes. His ultimate mistake is the horse. So there’s a sort of tragic flaw right from the beginning in our telling.

My interpretation of Zendaya’s character is that she is not Athena as Odysseus initially present her—gods don’t exist in this world—but a manifestation of his guilt. During the sack of Troy, we see her as a priestess in the Temple of Athena, and the Greeks behead her. For Odysseus, she encapsulates the chaos that the horse has wrought on the world. But my editor did not interpret it that way. I am hoping you will settle our disagreement.

I couldn’t possibly answer that because I learned very early on with Memento that it’s unfair to define the experience for the audience by answering questions like that. 

Here’s what I will say: For me, what was important was that we view the gods the way that people at the time might have viewed them. So they’re seeing evidence of the gods in nature. They’re seeking and finding gods and the influence of gods in the people around them. Odysseus says to Telemachus, “Don’t look for gods in men. You’ll just be disappointed.” And some of what Odysseus says about divinity, to me, is somebody who’s protesting a bit too much, someone trying to live in denial of their own instincts and their own practices. 

I was struck by the parallels between Oppenheimer and Odysseus, two brilliant men who create a tool of devastating destruction and then struggle with the guilt of what they have done. When I spoke to Matt Damon, I asked, “What did you think when you first read the script?” And he said, “It felt like Oppenheimer.” I assume that was a conscious choice.

Yes. If I’ve done a film right, it leaves me with questions. It leaves me with things I want to keep exploring and thinking about. And Oppenheimer fed very much into my reading of the story of Odysseus. 

John Leguizamo [who plays Odysseus’ friend Eumaeus] says it at the very beginning: “That’s very clever, but your cleverness will get you in trouble.” As it does again and again and again. This is where it ties into Oppenheimer: Just because you can doesn’t mean you should. The parallels were pretty apparent to me as I figured out how to adapt it. 

The movie hinges on this idea that by creating the Trojan Horse, Odysseus destroys “Zeus’ law.” That’s the movie’s term for the ancient Greek concept of xenia—the respectful relationship between host and guest—which can be tricky to explain to a modern audience. Why was it important to include?

When you find these things are difficult to deal with, sometimes the solution is just to dive in and make it everything. I didn’t use the term xenia because you don’t want to throw too many terms at people. But it’s essentially the golden rule. It all comes back to weather, to geography. When you leave the house, you are depending on the kindness of strangers, and you have to trust that when you arrive somewhere after weeks or months of traveling, that you will be fed, you will be given water. Three thousand years ago, that was everything. You were always at the mercy of strangers. And so this idea that a stranger could be a god in disguise, it’s very powerful as the underpinning of a belief system. 

At different points in the film, if man is given the opportunity, he becomes a beast. A soldier will behead a priestess. You imply that Menelaus purposefully scarred Helen’s face either because he believes she’s responsible for the Trojan War or to prevent anyone from taking her again.

That line, “The face that launched 1,000 ships, or maybe just 500” just occurred to me to write. Sometimes what you do as a writer is purely instinctive. I felt the poem didn’t necessarily address what it is for Helen to be brought back by Menelaus and how that would ever work. How would that relationship be? How could it possibly be anything other than the most acidic, awful marriage?

You don’t buy that he saw her face and said, “She’s so beautiful I can’t kill her after all,” as he does in the myth?

There’s a lot of sh-t that’s happened in that relationship, and we have a very brief moment of time with them in this story. I was looking for a shorthand way to communicate the aftermath of the war and how it’s been traumatic for the entire world. 

You also see this idea of man as beast in the scene with Circe. She says that Odysseus’ men would have raped and killed her—that they’re pigs. Then you get to the end and see the sack of Troy and the horror of what they did. She’s right.

Circe articulates it well in the film. I love the way Samantha [Morton] has played the part. Talking about choices of adaptation, the end of the poem is so grim and so misogynistic, I had to exclude some of that material. But I didn’t want to completely take it off the table in terms of what it is saying about men and the way they wage war. 

And yet you give Odysseus and Penelope a happy ending that they do not get in the poem.

Well, it is the fall of civilization, so there is a fairly bleak sensibility. The end is talking about cycles, and you can view cycles pessimistically: History is doomed to repeat itself. But there is also something optimistic about those cycles. As Penelope says, “Civilization will rise again.” There is rebirth and regrowth. 

For me, it was important in looking at the ending to try and strike the right balance between pessimism and optimism—pessimism about what might have precipitated the Bronze Age catastrophe and the optimism that positive things will reassert themselves.

item.title: Here Are the Candidates Vying for Sen. Lindsey Graham’s Seat
item.description: The race is looking crowded ahead of a key deadline for the special primary election to replace the late Senator on the November ballot.

media:content.media:description: Voting booths at a polling location inside the Charles R. Drew Wellness Center during a primary election in Columbia, South Carolina, on June 9, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
The deadline for candidates to file their intent to run in the special Republican primary election to fill the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s seat is next week, and the race is already looking quite crowded.

Graham, who represented South Carolina in the Senate for more than two decades, had been seeking his fifth term in the upper chamber before he died of an aortic dissection last week. Days after his death, South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster appointed Graham’s sister, Darline Graham Nordone, to finish out the remainder of his term, which ends in January.

Read More: What to Know About Lindsey Graham’s Funeral Services

Voters, meanwhile, will have the opportunity to pick a new Republican nominee to vie for a full term in his seat in the special Republican primary election on Aug. 11. 

Candidates have until July 28 to file their intent to run. Here are the candidates who have announced their plans to enter the race so far.

Darline Graham Nordone

Nordone told Fox News’ Sean Hannity in an interview released on Monday that she plans to run for a full term in her brother’s Senate seat. 

“I’m in,” she said during the interview.

A few days earlier, President Donald Trump urged Nordone to run for a full term.

“Darline, who comes from an absolutely incredible family, has been a WINNER all of her life and, should she accept, has my Complete and Total Endorsement in the Special Election for U.S. Senate in South Carolina,” Trump said in a Truth Social post last week.

Nordone, a mother of two, was a fervent supporter of her brother’s political career, but she herself had never before held public office. She spent years working in disabilities services.

Read More: Who is Darline Graham Nordone? Lindsey Graham’s Sister Appointed to Serve Out His Senate Term

Russell Fry

South Carolina Rep. Russell Fry also announced on Monday that he intends to run for the seat.

“Too many South Carolina families are struggling to make ends meet,” he said in a post on X. “We need a conservative fighter in the Senate who delivers real results. I will be your conservative MAGA candidate in the special primary Senate election this summer.”

Fry is also running for reelection for the House seat he currently holds. If he were to win both the Senate and House races, he would only be allowed to take on one of those roles.

Mark Sanford

Mark Sanford, a former South Carolina congressman and governor, said on Thursday that he will be entering the race to fill Graham’s seat.

“Our country is at a financial tipping point, and I can’t sit on the sidelines while Washington adds a trillion dollars to the debt every 100 days,” he said in a social media post. “I’ve spent my entire time in politics fighting this fight, and I’m running for U.S. Senate to keep the American dream alive for our sons, my grandson, and those you love.”

Sanford was at the center of a public scandal while serving as governor in 2009, when he admitted to having an extramarital affair. The admission came amid widespread doubts about his whereabouts one week that June, when his staff initially said that the governor was taking some time off to write and later that he was hiking the Appalachian Trail. Instead, he had traveled to Argentina in secret to visit his lover. 

Still, Sanford brushed off calls to resign and went on to finish his term as governor. Sanford, who held a seat in the House before he became governor, was later reelected to the lower chamber and went on to serve three more terms there.

He also previously mounted an unsuccessful 2020 presidential campaign.

Mark Lynch

On July 13, businessman Mark Lynch confirmed that he will run for Graham’s seat in the Senate.

“A lot of you have asked. Yes, it’s official,” he said in a social media post. “I’m committed to finish what God has called us to since February of 2025. To bring the U.S. Senate seat of South Carolina back to TRUE Conservative leadership for the Republican party.”

Lynch previously challenged Graham in the Republican primary race for the seat in the upper chamber. He ultimately lost the race to Graham in the June 9 primary election, but he earned the second highest share of the vote, with just under 29%.

Ralph Norman

South Carolina Rep. Ralph Norman announced on July 18 that he plans to enter the special Republican primary race.

“It’s official! I’m running to represent the people of South Carolina in the U.S. Senate because we need a fighter who will stand with President Trump and carry on Lindsey Graham’s legacy!” he said in a post on X.

On Thursday, Norman posted a video of himself and South Carolina Rep. Nancy Mace, in which she endorsed him in the race. Some people had previously speculated that Mace herself might launch a bid for Graham’s seat, but she announced earlier this week that she would not be running.

“This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to send a tried and true conservative to the United States Senate,” Mace said in the video Norman shared. “Ralph Norman doesn’t bend, he doesn’t break, and he doesn’t back down.”

Duke Buckner

Duke Buckner is also joining the race for Graham’s seat, according to local news outlet WIS News 10. Buckner has unsuccessfully run multiple campaigns to represent South Carolina in the House and Senate over the years.

“I am running because too many Americans are working harder and falling further behind,” Buckner told WIS News 10. “People should be able to afford a home, raise a family, and build a better life. We need to make it easier to build, expand opportunities in the skilled trades, and lower the cost of living.”

Mark McBride

Mark McBride—a former mayor of Myrtle Beach, South Carolina—said in a social media post on Wednesday that he had filed his intent to run in the Senate race the previous day.

In his post, McBride said that “a solid underlying platform” to his campaign was his disagreement with Trump launching the war in Iran.

“A vote on Tuesday, August 11th for Mark McBride is NOT a vote to continue to have our troops as sitting ducks in uninhabitable, destroyed former U.S. Bases in the Middle East,” he said. “A vote for Mark McBride is for a new direction for the Republican Party.”

Samuel Shepherd

Samuel Shepherd, who is a biochemical and medical engineer, also joined the crowded race this week, according to South Carolina Public Radio.

Clark Neilson

Clark Neilson, a land surveyor who appears to live in Charlotte, filed his intent to run in the special election as well, according to South Carolina Public Radio. He told the local news outlet that he had been thinking about running for office for a while.
