item.title: Mary Steenburgen Does Not Feel Bad if You Lost Your Tennis Court to Pickleball
item.description: The veteran actress on her new comedy 'The Dink'

media:content.media:description: Mary Steenburgen and Jake Johnson in The Dink

item.content:encoded:
Pickleball, as you might have heard, has in recent years been considered the fastest-growing sport in America. So the combination of the sport’s name, how it’s played—on a tiny court, with a ping-pongish racket, and a wiffle-ish plastic ball—and surging popularity makes it ripe for parody.

Enter The Dink, a new comedy directed by Josh Greenbaum (Barb and Star Go to Vista Del Mar, Will & Harper), co-produced by Ben Stiller, and starring Mary Steenburgen, Ed Harris, and Jake Johnson. The film, which debuts on Apple TV on July 24, serves as a sweet ode to this burgeoning pastime, while still poking fun at its foibles. For example, the cast, which also includes Stiller, the late Lynne Marie Stewart, Aaron Chen, Chloe Fineman, and Cleo King, offers intentionally corny, and thus amusing, jokes about “the kitchen,” the pickleball zone in front of the net that participants absolutely cannot enter to hit volleys. 

TIME caught up with Steenburgen, the Oscar winner and comedy stalwart—and real-life pickleball enthusiast—to talk about the sport, The Dink, and a humanitarian cause dear to her heart. 

(This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity)

When and why did you start playing pickleball?

About two months before I knew anything about The Dink, my son Charlie McDowell gave me a paddle and said, "Mom, I've had women even older than you whip my ass.” I said, “That's such a sweet thing to say.” He gave me some lessons. He's been my encouragement. And I started taking lessons on Martha's Vineyard by a woman named Connie McHugh, who's an incredible coach and teacher, and she helped me to just fall in love with it. I saw in it something that I could do at this age that I could get good at–maybe not great at or world-class, but good at–and go have fun with friends, and feel like I had a sport, which I hadn't had since my 40s, when I did start swimming competitively. I've missed having that feeling. So I started feeling that feeling again, of learning something with my body. I like puzzles a lot. Pickleball has a lot of puzzle aspects to it. Because it's not just about power. It's about finesse. It's about angles. It's about remembering all the little ways that you can trip yourself up. So I love what it does to how I think in my brain. And then I've made friends that I never would have known, people I never would have met, through this sport. 

About two months into this happy journey, when I was about to close a deal on a different project, my agents and managers called and said, "Well, there's one more offer for you, and we should probably tell you about it.” And I said, "What is it?” And they said, "Well, it shoots in L.A.” I go, "OK.” And they go, "It's with Josh Greenbaum and Jake Johnson and Ben Stiller.” And I went, "You're kidding.” So obviously it's a comedy, and it's a lead. And it's about pickleball. I went, “That's the one I'm gonna do.” “No, you have to read it first.” And I go, “I'll read it, but that's the one I'm gonna do.” It honestly felt like somebody in heaven just designed it for me.

Why do you think pickleball has gotten so popular in the last five, six years or so?

Because it's sort of egalitarian. All ages can play. Any body type can play. You don't have to be one of these extraordinary athletes. You can be a regular person and play at a level that will bring you pleasure and joy. And the hardest part is learning all the byzantine scoring and the rules and stuff. Also in my case, it was really finding people that were at a great level for me to play. That were hopefully a little bit better than me, so I would grow, but not so much better that they'd be bored playing with me. And I've found that now. So it's really fun for me.

The movie plays on a real conflict that's happened across the country: the fight over space. Pickleball’s expansion has required the need, for example, for the sport to take over tennis courts in some places, ruffling feathers. Full disclosure: I’ve felt this firsthand. I play tennis recreationally and basketball recreationally with my son, and pickleball's encroached on our space a little bit. Do you have sympathy for us folks on the other side of this conflict?

Not really. [Laughs.] I don't think we're trying to do this for no reason. We're trying to do this because of the best reason, which is it's really fun. Do I want the sport of tennis, or God forbid, the sport of basketball to ever go away? No. Tennis is elegant. And basketball is, oh my God, a magical sport full of heart and brilliance. And there's room for all of it. Do we all have to keep fighting over things when all of it is actually quite holy because it gives people something to do that's good for them and brings them joy? In the case of basketball, it's you and your son out there. I played pickleball with both my granddaughters last week and learned something about both of them. There is a holy thing to that. I don't think we have to choose between things that are fun.

One of the film’s comedic bits is your character and Jake Johnson’s character playing against a team in which both players grunt loudly on the court. Are there really pickleball grunters? 

I've heard it in pickleball. And it amuses me even more in pickleball than tennis because in tennis, legitimately it's a long way from one side to the other. But with pickleball, it's not that far. You don't have to grunt.

Did you need a pickleball double for the film?

They had a double for me, and she's since become a friend of mine. And she's quite an extraordinary double because she was the No. 1 player in the world over 50. And her name is Beth Bellamy. Her son Roscoe is the No. 6 singles player in the world. My son and I have played with them. I played with Roscoe Bellamy, and he played with Beth Bellamy. And the funniest thing was watching the mother and son smash it at each other. I mean, so hard. And my son and I were looking at each other like, “I wouldn't dare do that.” They're high-level athletes. They're amazing, and it was hilarious to watch them. 

They used her in two-shots. It's pretty much mostly me. I watch it and wish could do it all over again because I play better now than I did then. But that's OK.

Do you play with your husband, Ted Danson? 

I do not. He will not play with me. He has a bad shoulder. He doesn't want to talk about it, and he won't play with me. But I have plenty of people to play with. 

So another line that stood out in the movie was, somebody said something along the lines of, “You can learn to play pickleball in an hour.” And then the response was, “As if that's a good thing.” What's your reply to that notion that pickleball is too easy?

Well, it's not exclusive. And there's a lot of exclusivity now, and not enough inclusivity. Anything that brings people together and makes them laugh is a good thing. And by the way, no one can learn the scoring thing and all the rules in an hour. It is so cockamamie and crazy. I'm still learning.

On a bittersweet note, Lynne Marie Stewart, who played Miss Yvonne on the groundbreaking Saturday-morning TV show Pee Wee’s Playhouse, plays one of your pickleball friends in the film. Stewart died of cancer in February 2025, a few months after filming wrapped. What was it like working with her?

I adored her. There was absolutely no sign of her being ill. I know she didn't know, and then several weeks after the film, she became very ill. And the sweet thing I would tell you is that Jake and Josh took a rough cut of the film to hospice and showed it to her, as the last film she saw before she passed. She loved it and she saw how good she was in it. I think it was very meaningful for her that she got to do it and she got to see it.

You appeared in Elf, a stone-cold Christmas classic. And you actually ate the spaghetti and maple syrup concoction favored by Will Ferrell’s elfin character. What did that taste like?

Exactly what you think. I don't recommend it. It's not the worst thing I've ever eaten. Maple syrup makes everything better. But it's not what your taste buds want out of spaghetti.

You also worked with Will Ferrell in Step Brothers. What stands out about that experience?

One thing is there was a phone call from Will Ferrell to me. I remember I was in my house on Martha's Vineyard, and he called me himself out of the blue. We had done Elf the year before. I think it was the year before. And he said, “I know you played my stepmom in Elf. Would you be offended if I asked you to play my actual mom?” And I said, "Well, let me do the math here.” And I asked him when he was born. Then I go, "Well, Will, I would have had to have had you when I was 11. [Editor’s note: Steenburgen is 73. Ferrell is 59.] But the answer is, ‘I would be offended if you ask anybody else because I definitely want to do it.’” Because he and I had such a good time together on Elf. 

But on the first day of Step Brothers, what he and John C. Reilly were doing was so high-level, off-the-charts, insane, bonkers, brilliant, that Richard Jenkins, who's an extraordinary actor, and I looked at each other and went, "What the hell are we doing here?” And I think both of us had this kind of crazy feeling, like, “I can't do that.” And so I went home that night, and I really thought about it, and I came back the next day, and I said, “Richard, I figured it out. I know what we're doing here.” And he said, “What?” I said, “It is our job to hold down the truth that these two grown idiots are living at home with them. We have to make that real.”

At the 2025 Emmys, you and Ted received the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award. You’ve both been active in a variety of causes, including anti-apartheid in South Africa, research for pediatric AIDS, and the importance of arts in public schools. On the philanthropic/humanitarian front, is there anything new you're working on that’s exciting or interesting or important to you?

There is. I once knew two doctors that I met through the White House Fellows Program many years ago, and they had a little boy named Sam. And when I met him, he was 3, and Sam looked about 95 because Sam had progeria, which is premature aging syndrome. I became friends with this little boy and remained friends with him throughout his all-too-short life. He lived to be a teenager and passed away some years ago. But his mother, who was a doctor, got herself put on the Human Genome Project, and she, along with Dr. Francis Collins, found the gene variant for progeria, which is amazing. Not only did they do that, but they, through the Progeria Research Foundation, have found a method of gene editing, and a little device that carries that into the organs of the body, that can go in mice and reedit genes to where someone with progeria today can actually get better. If it works with progeria, there's a chance that all these rare and deeply underfunded diseases that more people should care about could actually be alleviated from the face of the earth. So I am trying to help them because they need to raise about $20 to $25 million to get this first patient to have this. 

You’ve had such a long and varied career: you’ve won an Oscar and played all different types of roles in dramas and comedies. Is there any role you haven't played that you still want to do? Any bucket-list items, career-wise?

I've never done Shakespeare. I've never done some of the great Southern kind of plays that I probably should have done. I balance what I do between my family and work and my marriage, but I also have a very important career to me that's quite separate, which is I write music. I'm working on some things now that are really important to me. I don't look at anything about my career with any disappointment. I look at all of it with gratitude. It's crazy to me still that I get to do this. I constantly feel the need to prove myself and to get better. One of the things I love about it is that I don't have a plan. I feel like what's meant to be mine is going to come my way.

You mentioned music. You’ve talked about how, after minor arm surgery in 2007, you started hearing music in your mind all the time. What exactly happened there, where a medical procedure made you musical? 

I had a surgery on my right arm that was very innocuous, except they did put me under for it. I'll never know for sure, but we think they let my blood pressure get too low, and I had a little bit of a brain event. Not a serious thing. All I felt when I woke up was weird. So I assumed I'm just getting the anesthetic out of my body. But days later, I still felt weird, and you know, no one was helpful about what was going on with me. And Ted kept saying, "You seem like you can't focus on what I'm saying.” And I said, "Well, I can't focus because of the music.” And he's like, "There's no music playing.” I go, "Well, there's music playing in here.” [Points to head.]

People say it was a gift. It might have been a gift, but it was a gift I had to work really hard to harness and make sense out of. My grandmother was extremely musical, so I don't know if I just got to some part of my brain that was there that I hadn't. I don't know enough about the brain. But I became obsessed with music, and from the obsession, I started studying music. My first instrument was an accordion, which I just started playing. It didn't take me long to figure it out. And then I consumed books about songwriting and started paying attention to song structure. All this work helped to calm it down to the point where I could behave like a normal person. But I am still absolutely obsessed with music, and particularly with writing music. I write mostly with people from or connected to Nashville, because I'm signed with Universal Music Publishing Group in Nashville, and I really love the Nashville way of writing and the seriousness about musicianship and writing. I just love my friends there. So we're doing some crazy, wonderful things. We just got through writing two end-credit songs for movies. I enjoy it very much.

Very cool. Closing up on The Dink – what do you want people to take away from the film?

I hope they laugh in a summer where laughter is probably a really good thing. I hope some of them safely go out and have fun playing pickleball and don't hurt themselves. I hope that it reminds people in the business that these smaller films that are beautifully written, with a great script, have value in the marketplace. And in a dream world, maybe we'll get to do another one. That would make me very happy

Dink is a name for a pickleball drop shot. How’s your dink?

My dink is pretty good. I dinked against Anna Leigh Waters this morning, and although there were three of us playing one person, we did win best two out of  three from my little dink.

And last question: Why the hell do they call it “the kitchen”?

I have no idea.

item.title: Meet Marie-France van Heel, Wife of Britain's New Prime Minister Andy Burnham
item.description: From an appearance on a famous U.K. dating show to her career in marketing, here's an introduction to the lesser-known new occupant of No. 10 Downing Street.

media:content.media:description: Marie-France van Heel alongside her husband Prime Minister Andy Burnham, arriving at Downing Street in London, United Kingdom, on July 20, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
When the U.K.’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived at 10 Downing Street earlier this week, his wife of 25 years, Marie-France van Heel, was right by his side.

The couple, who share a son and two daughters, met at university, where van Heel was “much more high-flying” than Burnham, according to an interview the lawmaker gave in 2009.

Burnham, 56, has publicly thanked his wife for the “sacrifice” she made early on in his political career when he earned his first parliamentary selection for the northern England town of Leigh in 2001.

“When my wife got pregnant, we actually hadn't planned to have children at that time because I felt stability was important,” Burnham said. “We got married in October 2000, when Jimmy [our eldest child] was eight months old, and I was in a difficult battle to win the nomination. It was horrendous, up and down the M6 [motorway] from London campaigning.” 

Burnham’s wife has been a constant source of support throughout his political career, which saw him unsuccessfully vie for Labour leadership on two separate occasions before running unchallenged earlier this month.

The Burnham-van Heel family have laid strong roots in the north of England, where the now-Prime Minister served as mayor of Greater Manchester until last month, when he made a triumphant return to Westminster after winning the Makerfield by-election.

Having built a successful career in marketing, van Heel previously worked as chief strategy officer for consultancy firm Heavenly, which has worked on brand campaigns for the BBC, HSBC, and England Rugby. 

According to the BBC, she now serves as chief marketing officer at Iduna Infrastructure, a company which owns significant parts of Manchester's electric vehicle charging network.

During his mayoral tenure, Burnham chose to declare his wife's links to EV charging and remove himself from any related decision-making "so that there could be no perception of a conflict of interest nor any suggestion of privileged information being misused.”


Now, as he takes on the challenge of being the U.K.’s seventh Prime Minister in a decade, Burnham will come under a new spotlight. Here’s what to know about the person supporting him behind the scenes.

Marie-France van Heel appeared on a famous U.K. dating show

The Prime Minister has credited his time studying at Cambridge University for many of his good fortunes, including meeting his wife.

Burnham studied English and was in his second year when he bonded with van Heel, a Dutch-born peer.

During a Labour leadership hustings in July 2015, Burnham revealed an interesting detail about the earlier years of their relationship.

When the candidates were asked what made them human, Burnham regaled a story of his wife appearing on the former hit romance show Blind Date in the early 90s after he gave her his blessing.

The premise of the show saw a “picker” given the chance to ask questions to three potential suitors, all hidden behind a screen, before eventually picking one to go on a date with. The couple would then return to the show the following week, to let the host and audience know how the date went.

“In the early days, she was on Blind Date and she was the picker,” he said, according to The Spectator. “And to add insult to injury, she picked Will from Surrey, who ended up being the director of communications for the Conservative Party.”

The man in question was Will Harris, who did indeed go on to serve as the chief marketing officer for the Conservatives.

Luckily for Burnham, van Heel and Harris failed to find a spark on their date and swiftly went their separate ways.

Burnham has had the support of his wife from the beginning of his political career

Burnham told van Heel on the first night they met that he wanted to be an MP [Member of Parliament].

“I met him on my first day at university. Yes, with the long hair, the good looks, and monobrow,” van Heel recalled in a 2015 interview. When Burnham told her of his political aspirations, van Heel “left the room,” but they soon formed a burgeoning relationship. 

When he was considering running for the Labour leadership contest in 2015, Burnham had his family at the forefront of his mind.

“We talked it through and it was very much a team effort, a family effort. I wouldn’t put them through it if I wasn’t sure,” he said.

Van Heel’s family experience with cancer 

Burnham previously served as Health Secretary under the premiership of Gordon Brown from 2009 to 2010, then as the shadow Health Secretary following Labour’s defeat in the 2010 general election. 

It was during this role that he revealed the challenging personal experience he and his wife had faced. 

"It's been a devastating few years. You couldn't imagine a crueller set of circumstances happening to any family," said Burnham in 2010.

Van Heel had undergone a pre-emptive double mastectomy after learning she carried the gene for breast cancer following the death of her sister Claire from the disease, and the diagnosis of both her mother Bea and other sister, Louise. 

“As hard as it was to take, the decision was liberating rather than depressing, because it's lifted the cloud of fear,” said Burnham of his wife’s surgery. 

Van Heel has since participated in Cancer Research UK’s Race for Life event.

item.title: Tick Bites Are Causing Red-Meat Allergies. What to Know About Alpha-Gal Syndrome
item.description: Alpha-gal syndrome is a strange tick-borne illness that induces an allergy to a specific type of sugar found in red meat.

media:content.media:description: An adult female lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum) crawls on a blade of grass. Image courtesy CDC. (Photo by Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)

item.content:encoded:
Doctors in the U.S. are hearing an odd complaint from their patients more frequently: lifelong meat eaters are suddenly breaking out into hives, getting bad stomach pains, and are sometimes vomiting or having diarrhea after eating red meat.

The symptoms are typical of alpha-gal syndrome, a strange tick-borne illness first identified in the 2000s that induces an allergy to a specific type of sugar found in red meat. Most mammals (but not humans) have cells that contain the sugar, so it’s found in beef, lamb, and pork—all popular protein sources in the human diet.

Nearly 500,000 Americans are living with alpha-gal syndrome, according to estimates from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Researchers from Virginia Commonwealth University reported in 2025 that from 2013 to 2024, the number of positive tests for the alpha-gal antibody in people’s blood increased 100-fold, suggesting that more people have developed immune reactions to alpha gal, and are therefore allergic to it. In May, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced several initiatives against tick-borne diseases, including new research funding for alpha-gal syndrome.

Here's what to know about alpha-gal syndrome.

How do ticks cause alpha-gal syndrome?

In the U.S., the condition most commonly starts with a bite from a lone star tick, and less often from bites from a blacklegged tick or western blacklegged tick. When a tick bites a human, it releases viruses or bacteria (like the one that causes Lyme disease) as well as its saliva, which contains compounds to thin the blood and numb the bite area. It also contains alpha gal, which causes problems for some when it's released into their blood. “The tick is injecting alpha gal directly from its saliva into the blood, and the [human] body is not used to seeing alpha gal in this way,” says Dr. Bobbi Pritt, chair of clinical microbiology at the Mayo Clinic.

Since the sugar is not normally found in blood, some people’s immune systems recognize it as foreign and mount a vigorous defense to eliminate it by producing antibodies to alpha gal. Those antibodies are generally relatively harmless, cruising through the blood looking out for any alpha gal it may encounter. When people eat red meat, however, some of the alpha gal in the digested meat can be absorbed into the bloodstream, where the antibodies go to work.

In some people, this causes an allergic reaction. If the reaction escalates, it can lead to anaphylactic shock and even death.

Can eating any type of meat trigger alpha-gal syndrome?

Most mammals—but not humans—contain alpha gal, so someone with alpha-gal syndrome will likely have an allergic reaction to consuming meat from cows, pigs, lambs, goats, and deer. Even among these meats, some organ cuts like the liver, kidneys, sweetbreads, and intestines might be more likely to trigger an allergic reaction since they contain higher levels of alpha gal, according to the CDC.

What are the symptoms of alpha-gal syndrome?

The symptoms can vary, says Pritt, and they generally get worse every time you eat red meat. If you develop alpha-gal syndrome, the first time you eat a steak or burger after being bitten by a tick, you might get symptoms that are on the milder side, like a rash, itching, hives, or flushing several days later. Some people might experience swelling in the eyes and lips, she says. Others may get intestinal symptoms such as diarrhea, vomiting, or nausea.

For those who might be severely allergic, or for people with the allergy who continue to consume red meat, symptoms could intensify to include difficulty breathing, wheezing, or even anaphylactic shock. Because a severe allergic reaction is so dangerous, Pritt says, “you don’t want to face alpha-gal syndrome alone. There is the potential, especially after repeated exposure, of having a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction.”

Is alpha gal only found in red meat?

There may be hidden sources of alpha gal in products that rely on animal components. Dr. Mario Rodenas, associate professor of allergy and immunology at Yale University, says the syndrome can also occur among cancer patients taking the chemotherapy drug cetuximab, which includes a component made from mouse cells that contain alpha gal. Doctors first made the connection between tick bites and severe allergic reactions to the cancer drug in 2008, when they learned that cancer patients with higher levels of certain immune cells made them more sensitive to the alpha gal in the medication, and that their more sensitive immune systems were triggered by tick bites.

Pritt says other animal-based products, like dairy, butter, milk, lard and bone broth, may also contain alpha gal and could trigger an allergic reaction among people with the syndrome. Gelatin-containing products could also be a potential catalyst if they are made from animal products.

Can you eventually “grow out of” alpha-gal allergies, like you can other food allergies?

“Yes, that’s a bit of bright news in the picture,” says Pritt: Alpha-gal syndrome is not always permanent. But experts still don’t know enough about the syndrome and how it changes the body’s immune system to know for certain when and how people might be able to safely eat meat once they’ve developed the allergy.

That’s why it’s important to protect yourself from tick bites—especially if you’ve already been bitten in the past by a tick, since you won't always know which type of tick you encountered. “We learned that if you get frequent tick exposures, once you develop this [syndrome], if you get another tick exposure, it can bump up or increase the concentration of allergic antibodies against alpha gal,” says Rodenas. “So you’re perpetuating the problem. Some people have outgrown this because they avoided further tick bites. But we have to follow people [for longer] since we haven’t been able to so far, because the disease is so young.”

Why are more people developing alpha-gal syndrome now?

A few factors could explain why alpha-gal syndrome appears to be on the rise. First, increased awareness of the connection between tick bites and alpha-gal syndrome means more doctors are reporting it, and more people are asking their health care professionals about the condition.

Second, the expanding habitat of ticks could be leading to more bites and consequently more cases of the allergy. Warmer climates mean the tick primarily responsible, the lone star tick, has spread from the southern U.S. all the way through New England in the Northeast.

Rodenas is studying the factors that might contribute to someone developing alpha-gal syndrome. “We really don’t know what these patients look like,” he says. “We want to characterize what these patients’ comorbidities or other medical problems are, to try to better define who is a higher risk of developing this—is it younger people or older people? Men, women, or children?” He is including medical data in people’s health records extending back 12 years to detect patterns among those who develop the allergy.

Why don’t people develop alpha-gal syndrome simply from eating red meat?

The difference between being exposed to alpha-gal syndrome from eating red meat and from a tick bite has to do with where the alpha gal enters the body. When people eat red meat, most of the alpha gal is digested in the stomach and small intestine, with very little being absorbed into the blood. And any alpha gal that is absorbed after digestion will be in a different, already digested form, while the original version comes from tick saliva, says Pritt. With a tick bite, all of the carbohydrate is injected directly into the blood, where immune cells are on constant watch for anything unusual. In the blood, alpha gal triggers an immune response, while it generally doesn’t in the digestive tract.

Why do some people develop alpha-gal syndrome after a tick bite while others who get bitten don’t?

As with any allergy, alpha-gal syndrome occurs against the backdrop of a person’s existing immune reactions, and people have different sensitivities to various compounds. Tick saliva also contains a number of other immune-affecting compounds that can modify the immune system, says Pritt. Some people might be more prone to activating an immune component known as IgE, for example, which tends to stimulate other immune mechanisms involved in an allergic reaction. So those who already have higher levels of IgE patrolling the blood might be prone to developing alpha-gal syndrome than those with lower amounts.

item.title: 10 Foods That Food Safety Experts Never Eat
item.description: Some of their no-go foods are obvious. Others are probably in your fridge right now.
item.content:encoded:
Ask someone who investigates foodborne illness for a living what they won't put on their plate, and the list is shorter—and stranger—than you'd expect.

It's not that these experts live in fear. Most will tell you that all food carries some risk, and the real skill is deciding which risks are worth taking. Frank Yiannas, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s former deputy commissioner for food policy and response, says he doesn't think of foods as simply "good" or "bad." Instead, "I approach everything with what I would say is a quantitative risk assessment," he says. "I'm calculated."

Still, after decades of investigating outbreaks—and, in some cases, having their own lives forever changed by foodborne illness—these experts have each decided a handful of foods simply aren't worth the gamble. Some of their no-go items are predictable; others might be sitting in your fridge right now. Here’s what came up again and again.

Raw milk and raw-milk cheese

There's almost no debate about this one. "It's ridiculous," says Bill Marler, a food-safety lawyer who has spent decades suing companies over outbreaks. He says he has represented families of children who have died or suffered kidney damage and neurological complications after foodborne illness linked to raw milk, and to him, the risk simply isn't worth it. It’s especially hard to justify when there's a safe alternative. “You have such a great thing called pasteurization,” he says. 

"It’s very risky," says Barbara Kowalcyk, director of the Institute of Food Safety and Nutrition Security at George Washington University, who avoids raw milk and cheeses made from it. "We've known that for decades." 

Kowalcyk knows the stakes of food safety in a deeply personal way. In 2001, she lost her young son to complications from a foodborne E. coli infection—a tragedy that led her to leave a career in pharmaceutical research and devote her life to food safety. (She believes her son’s illness was caused by tainted ground beef in a hamburger he’d eaten.)

Cantaloupe

Ask Darin Detwiler to name some of the riskiest produce in the grocery store, and he doesn't hesitate: cantaloupe. "You cannot adequately clean the outside of the cantaloupe," says Detwiler, an associate teaching professor of food policy at Northeastern University and author of Food Safety: Past, Present, and Predictions. Once you run a knife through the rough rind, he says, you drag whatever's on the surface straight into the flesh.

If you love it anyway, his rule is to cut it and eat it right away—never let cut melon sit out for more than two hours. And he has one warning sign to watch for: cut melon that's been sitting too long can develop what looks like a dusting of powdered sugar on the surface. It isn't sugar. "That’s when the pathogens have grown so much you can actually see them," he says. He skips the fruit entirely. For Detwiler, some food risks simply aren't worth taking. After losing his young son in the 1993 Jack in the Box E. coli outbreak, he devoted his career to food safety.

Raw oysters and shellfish

Raw oysters show up on a lot of experts' no-go lists. Shellfish are filter feeders, Marler explains—they pull water through their bodies, and "anything in the water that's contaminated, they suck it into their bodies." If the water is contaminated, there's a good chance your oyster is, too.

Detwiler ranks oysters among his personal top three foods to avoid. (Marler does, too.) Beyond the contaminated water, Detwiler says, they're linked to frequent illness outbreaks and can be notoriously difficult to trace back to their source. 

Sushi rolls

Dr. Daniel Griffin, an infectious disease physician and president of Parasites Without Borders, doesn't swear off sushi entirely. He does eat it—but only after inspecting it. Some fish parasites are large enough to spot with the naked eye: thin, reddish, thread-like worms visible in a pale piece of fish. "If you Google 'fish with parasite,' you'll probably lose your appetite," he says. He examines each piece before eating it and skips rolls altogether. "I'm not gonna [eat] the roll with something hidden in there," he says.

Undercooked pork

Jill Roberts, a molecular epidemiologist and professor at the University of South Florida College of Public Health, says pork is one meat she approaches with extra caution. She avoids thick cuts like pork tenderloin because they're harder to cook all the way through. "All I can see is Toxoplasma," she says. The parasite, which can also be spread through cat feces, has increasingly been linked to undercooked pork. "I'm just out on that one."

Sprouts

Raw sprouts are another easy pass for Kowalcyk. They've been linked to a long string of foodborne illness outbreaks, she says, "and there's really no good way to clean them." That's because contamination often starts before the sprouts are even grown: Bacteria can be present on the seeds themselves, and the warm, humid conditions needed for sprouting are also ideal for helping those bacteria multiply. Simply rinsing them under water isn't enough to reliably remove them. Cooking would make them safer—but then, she points out, you've lost the crunch that made them appealing in the first place. 

Pre-cut fruits and vegetables

Pre-cut fruits and vegetables are another easy pass. The convenience of a tub of pre-sliced melon or a bag of shredded carrots isn't worth giving up control over how your food is handled, Marler says. "You don't know how long it's been sitting around, or whether the knife, the cutting surface, or the hands that touched it were clean," he says.

Kowalcyk feels the same way. She'd rather buy produce whole and cut it herself than trust someone else to do it.

Raw eggs

Eggs are far safer today than they were 20 years ago, Marler notes—but he still won't eat them raw. That means no tasting cookie dough made with raw eggs, no licking brownie batter off the beaters, and no homemade Caesar dressing made with uncooked yolks. Most eggs sold in grocery stores aren't pasteurized, he notes, so if a recipe calls for raw eggs, he'd rather use pasteurized ones—or skip it altogether.

Undercooked hamburgers

A medium-rare steak and a medium-rare burger may look similar, but Griffin says they're completely different from a food-safety perspective. With a steak, bacteria generally stay on the surface, where cooking kills them. Grind that same meat into a hamburger, though, and any bacteria get mixed throughout the patty.

"You're gonna take whatever bacterial contamination, E. coli, or fecal contamination, and now you're gonna mix it all deep in there," he says.

That's why Griffin always orders burgers well done. Yiannas does too. At home, he uses a food thermometer instead of relying on color alone.

Potlucks and picnic foods

Roberts is wary of foods prepared outside regulated kitchens. "If it's a potluck, I'm out," she says. "If it's a bake sale, no." When coworkers organize a potluck, she jokes that she suddenly has another commitment. "I'm always ill," she says.

Family cookouts are a different story, because she can watch the food being grilled. Even then, she's vigilant about anything that sits out in the summer heat. Rather than leaving a big bowl of potato salad on the picnic table, she has her family keep most of it in the refrigerator and bring out only a small portion at a time, refilling the bowl as needed. Her sister now teases her by asking, "Do you want me to get an aliquot?"—a laboratory term Roberts has turned into family shorthand for serving a small batch.

item.title: The Robots Cometh
item.description: The humanoid revolution is coming—and the Chinese firm Unitree is leading the charge.
item.content:encoded:
Spectators typically leave a UFC fight with ringing ears and a sheepish resolve to get back to the gym. Wang Xingxing went straight to his laboratory. 

“I thought I could make a bigger robot for boxing competitions,” says Wang, the founder and CEO of Hangzhou-based humanoid-robotics firm Unitree. “Then I thought, Why not do an even bigger one that can actually carry a human inside?”

The upshot of Wang’s creative fervor is the GD01, which Unitree bills as the world’s first mass-produced, transformable mecha robot. Standing 9 ft. tall and weighing half a ton, it can transport a pilot in its torso-mounted cockpit, walk on either two legs or four, and wield fists powerful enough to knock down walls. Heavy-duty mechanical hinges connect titanium-alloy limbs to a protective casing of carbon fiber, enabling smooth, deliberate strides on brutish red legs.

Wang showed off the GD01 exclusively to TIME as part of his first international media interview, revealing that beyond mixed martial arts, he took a dash of inspiration from James Cameron: “We actually drew some references from a similar robot featured in Avatar.”

Wang has done more than arguably anyone else to bring this science fiction closer to reality. A native of China’s coastal city of Ningbo, he founded Unitree in 2016 when he was just 26 years old and has moved from robot dogs to humanoid robots and now, with GD01, human mobility machines. But while the GD01 might inspire awe, humbler humanoids like Unitree’s flagship G1 are the ones set to become the workhorses of a global robotics transformation already gathering pace in China, the U.S., and beyond.

This is the next great tech frontier, one that has previously been the purview of Star Wars and Blade Runner: AI that walks, sees, hears and physically interacts with the real world. Morgan Stanley predicts that as many as 13 million humanoids could walk among us by 2035—equivalent to the population of Bolivia. That number is forecast to rise to 1 billion by 2050, when the industry could be worth $5 trillion. 

Unitree is hardly alone staking a claim in this space. In January, Tesla announced the third generation of its Optimus humanoid robot with a goal to eventually produce 10 million units per year at factories in Fremont and Texas. In late June, California-based Figure dispatched its latest 03 humanoid to BMW’s Spartanburg plant in South Carolina, where its earlier 02 model helped assemble 30,000 cars last year. Oregon-based Agility, meanwhile, has secured deployments everywhere from Toyota to Latin American e-commerce giant Mercado Libre. But Unitree is the world leader in terms of volume, dispatching more than 5,500 units in 2025, comprising over a quarter of a global market that is only just waking. In June, Nvidia announced that its bleeding-edge Jetson Thor chip would be fitted into Unitree’s H2 humanoid for sale to research institutions around the globe. 

We could be, Wang says, anything from two to 10 years away from a “ChatGPT moment” for humanoids, whereby a robot achieves sufficient “generalization” to be able to execute 80% of requested voice commands in an 80% unfamiliar environment. “Once the technology surpasses this ... inflection point, robots can gradually be rolled out for large-scale commercial use,” he says.

If the timeline for that breakthrough is a matter of debate, its potential impact is not. Nonunion robots (the only kind) could operate around the clock on assembly lines, replace some nurses in hospitals, and pick fruit under the hot sun. 

The positive outlook is that wide-scale humanoid adoption will herald an unprecedented era of global abundance, automating mundane and dangerous labor while ushering in post-scarcity societies. There is a less rosy divination, however. Amid a mass labor displacement, robots concentrate even more wealth into fewer human hands. With production severed from wages, people could face an identity crisis as robots begin to dominate manual labor and service industries, while governments contend with strained social safety nets and rising competition between the U.S. and China—leaders in humanoids as they are in AI—over raw material and technology. On June 3, three U.S. lawmakers introduced the bipartisan Guard Act, which seeks to ban Chinese robots deemed to be a national-security threat. Unitree was singled out by John Moolenaar, a bill co-sponsor and chairman of the House Select Committee on China, who accused Wang’s firm of benefiting from “generous state subsidies” and threatening to bankrupt American competitors.

With AI, we’ve already seen how the ability of large language models (LLM) to parse huge reams of data also makes them susceptible to hallucinations and unintended consequences, like designing biological weapons. But while an LLM can suggest harm, a robot can enact it, auguring a terrifying new cybersecurity peril in the age of embodied AI. Online scams already siphon off staggering sums, but a hacked humanoid could move the threat from screens into homes, streets, nurseries, and factory floors.

The tension between these visions can be reduced to a choice of myth: Are Wang and his GD01, and indeed their competitors, akin to Luke Skywalker and the faithful, guileless C-3PO—or more like Frankenstein and his monster?

Wang, unsurprisingly, veers toward the positive, predicting that in 10 years every household may have a small robot that can do your laundry, grill your steak, and even provide basic care if you fall ill. They can also take on tasks most humans would rather avoid, from steep mountain farming to sewer maintenance.

But if that sounds like a future arriving faster than society can absorb it, Wang insists the transition will be gradual. “It will evolve step-by-step,” he says. “If society finds that robots don’t perform well in a certain sector, or if people simply don’t like them there, we can easily pivot and re-direct their application to other fields. So, everything remains well within controllable boundaries.”

Wang is an unlikely prophet of the AI age. Slight and bespectacled, he possesses none of the performative bravado associated with many technology founders. Instead, he speaks about robotics with quiet, unwavering conviction.

The possibilities and promises of a humanoid revolution have occupied him since he was 10 years old and first watched early televised robotics experiments performed at MIT by Marc Raibert, founder of Boston Dynamics. He spent his free time building model aircraft, conducting experiments, and, before long, assembling miniature turbojet engines. 

In 2009, Wang enrolled at Zhejiang Sci-Tech University in Hangzhou, majoring in mechatronics engineering. As a first-year student, he says, he built his first small bipedal robot, capable of walking a few steps, on less than $30. That same price-conscious approach would underpin Unitree’s flourishing. While pursuing a master’s degree at Shanghai University, he developed a prototype quadruped robot, XDog, which still occupies pride of place in the Unitree headquarters. Departing from the hydraulic-powered designs popularized by his idols at Boston Dynamics, Wang opted for a cost-saving electric-motor model, which helped XDog win second prize in a national entrepreneurship competition.

After graduation and a stint at Shenzhen-based drone trailblazer DJI, Wang launched Unitree with 2 million RMB ($300,000) in capital from an angel investor. It has since become a cultural phenomenon; an estimated 600 million people watched videos of Unitree’s H2 and G1 humanoid robots swinging nunchucks and executing flips as part of February’s Spring Festival Gala—China’s equivalent to the Super Bowl halftime show. It was the second year that Unitree humanoids provided the headline act, and all eyes are on what Wang has planned next time. “I have no idea,” he confesses with a laugh.

In March, Unitree filed for an IPO that would value the firm at $6 billion, sparking a buying frenzy in mainland Chinese markets for companies that would benefit along with it, such as upstream suppliers.

But high expectations are both a blessing and a curse. While Unitree’s first-quarter revenue surged over 68% year-on-year to $62 million, adjusted net profit halved over the same period to just $6 million, which the company blamed on a significant spike in R&D and sales costs. Wang talks about “a flip side” to viral internet fame. “Because the hype gets so intense, it places a fair amount of pressure on our company and the industry as a whole,” he says. “Everyone starts expecting your technology to leap forward at a breakneck pace. But the truth is, deep tech breakthroughs require a certain amount of time.”

Unitree’s blossoming came just as the Chinese government began leaning into AI and robotics, which President Xi Jinping has highlighted as key examples of the “new growth drivers.” China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology in turn declared humanoids a “disruptive innovation” on the same level as smartphones and EVs—breakthroughs destined to transform human production and lifestyle, making leadership a matter of economic and national security. It’s a policy push backed by hard cash; since late 2024, Chinese cities have put together investment funds worth over $26 billion, according to Morgan Stanley. Unitree hasn’t disclosed the exact level of state support it receives, though as one of Hangzhou’s “Six Little Dragons”—elite local startups—it benefits from the city’s $14 billion Sci-Tech Fund. “China is an ass kicker, next level,” Elon Musk told a Tesla earnings call in January. “To the best of our knowledge, we don’t see any significant [humanoid robot] competitors outside of China.”Wang’s role leading that charge was evident when he appeared as the youngest member of a high-profile business symposium hosted by Xi last spring. More than 140 Chinese companies now make humanoid robots, yet the perception inside China is that Unitree is not just another robotics startup, but a hardware platform destined to replicate what BYD achieved for EVs and DJI did for drones. Wang’s strategy is simple but hard to beat: first, control the most difficult core components; leverage scale to relentlessly drive down costs; and use each product generation to unlock new markets.

Unitree has slashed the pretax price of its flagship G1 humanoid from $16,000 to $13,500 in just 18 months. (Still, with components that cost under $9,000, according to recent estimates by SemiAnalysis, that gives Unitree a handy 33% gross margin.) The R1 model now retails for under $5,000, and over six years the price of their “robot dogs” has dropped from $45,000 to under $2,000. Wang insists Unitree wins through manufacturing cost efficiency—for example, it produces its own actuators, the “muscles” responsible for movement, which account for 50% to 70% of a humanoid’s cost. 

While the G1 might not boast the peak performance of some Western competitors in terms of load bearing and durability, it has crossed the “good enough” threshold for real-world deployment. With the ability to carry 5-kg payloads for 10 to 15 minutes continuously without overheating, it is moving out of R&D labs and into pilot deployments for warehouse logistics and material handling.

That said, to date only a fraction of humanoids sold are employed in actual useful work. The reason is very simple: today’s robots operate at about 30% to 50% of human efficiency for general factory and warehouse tasks, such as stacking and carrying boxes. Only 9% of Unitree’s sales go directly into industrial applications, with 17% for commercial venues such as tourist sites, exhibitions, and retail stores. That leaves 74% of Unitree’s humanoid sales to universities, research institutions, and individual developers looking to hone their own AI and motion-control capabilities. And the company is far from alone. The entire modern humanoid industry is essentially selling robots to people trying to build better robots. “Humanoid robots are just not ready for the mass market,” says Grace Shao, who publishes the AI Proem newsletter. 

Wang is unconcerned, however, and compares this trend to the early days of the personal computer, when they were primarily purchased by those in the business: “As the software becomes increasingly mature, with more developers joining each year, the proportion of genuine industrial deployments is growing at an incredibly fast pace.”

For now, Unitree is still wrestling with the same white whale as its legion of competitors: the generalization gap, which Wang calls “the biggest headache for the entire global scientific community.” While today’s back-flipping machines are engineering marvels, they remain stubbornly task-specific. If you want a robot to pick up a pen and move it across a desk, you must program every granular motion. But to make AI truly useful in the physical world, robots must transition from executing rigid scripts to understanding novel commands—like being told to simply “go to the grocery store.”

Achieving this milestone will require overcoming two self-reinforcing problems: the scarcity of 3D data and the diversity of deployment environments. Unlike LLMs like ChatGPT, which can parse the virtually boundless internet, robots need manipulation data collected in the real physical world, which is costly and difficult to scale. It must typically be collected manually by repetitively training machines how to perform certain tasks, such as folding shirts, stocking refrigerators, or shaking a mai tai. Plus, explains Jiang Zheyuan, CEO of Beijing-based humanoid firm Noetix, “even if a well-performing manipulation strategy is trained for a specific task, the success rate often drops sharply when the environment changes slightly—for example, object displacement, different lighting, or different tabletop materials.” 

Thanks to firms like Unitree, the hardware for humanoids is advancing quickly. The real battleground is over the robot brains, or vision-language-action (VLA) models, which are designed to turn human inputs into embodied AI performing intuitively and accurately. The VLA space alone will be worth $40.50 billion by 2035, predicts Kaiso Research, a market intelligence firm, and many of tech’s biggest players are aggressively pursuing their own models, including Nvidia’s GR00T N1.7, Google DeepMind’s RT-2-X, and Alibaba’s Qwen Robot Suite.

That battle is increasingly about one thing: collecting data. In New York City, for example, Micro AGI, which counts Unitree as a partner, is sending camera-wearing staff to clean apartments free of charge simply to generate 3D data to train its physical AI model. But as a dedicated robotics company, Unitree is arguably in a weaker position than Tesla, Xiaomi, or XPeng, which have diversified revenue streams and established supply chains. So solving this generalization gap is key to maintaining its status as today’s market champion. After all, its absolute sales are by any measure minuscule, meaning whoever closes the gap first could easily surge ahead.

There may be a game changer on the horizon: revolutionary new 6G connectivity would enable AI-native networks on which collective learning happens seamlessly across millions of connected devices. If one humanoid in a distant warehouse wrestles with a novel tool and finally masters it, that newly generated data can be instantly uploaded and shared across the entire global fleet. 6G will empower us “to make a digital twin of the world,” Cristiano Amon, CEO of $200 billion semiconductor firm Qualcomm, tells TIME. 

Boosted connectivity would solve the robotics bottlenecks of weight and battery life. Navigating our world requires simultaneously processing 4K video, spatial lidar, audio, and delicate tactile or proprioceptive feedback. But carrying heavy computational hardware and the means to power it severely limits both robot agility and operating time. 6G could potentially combine cloud processing with network lag of a near instantaneous 0.1 to 1 millisecond. Suddenly, lightweight physical robots could be animated by a cloud-based AI brain operating in real time. When a robot fumbles, 6G provides a safety net via remote human teleoperation.

As these machines come online, a significant challenge will be securing any centralized network. Last year, cybersecurity analysts discovered a “backdoor” in Unitree’s Go1 robot dogs, whereby third parties could log onto a portal to see the robot’s location, view live camera feeds, and even control it remotely. In response, Unitree shut down the cloud service that enabled the breach. Wang insists his “robot products operate completely disconnected from the network. If the client does not permit it, the robot will not save any environmental information whatsoever.” Besides, he adds, the data stored on a robot is “entirely negligible” when compared with that kept on a smartphone.

Then there is the fear, familiar from fiction, that machines built to act on our behalf might one day be made to act against us. Even today’s robots have shown physical AI carries physical risk: viral clips capture Unitree machines swinging an arm or a leg into unsuspecting children who stray into the path of their choreography. As humanoids graduate to generalization, whether they’ll become more cautious or more dangerous is a key question facing the industry. Wang plays down the potential for renegade robots to wreak havoc. “That won’t happen,” he says. “These robots are engineered with rigorous hardware constraints and safety protections.” 

The need for safety will hit home if human-shaped machines step off assembly lines and into living rooms. On June 30, Shenzhen-based UBtech launched its lifelike U1 humanoids specifically for companionship, featuring silicone skin and biomimetic facial expressions, and powered by what the company claims is world’s first empathic LLM “capable of recognizing more than 20 fine-grained emotional states.”

But the greatest obstacle to the household humanoid may not be technical. First proposed by Japanese roboticist Masahiro Mori in 1970, the “uncanny valley” hypothesis posits that as an object becomes more humanlike, our affection for it grows. Once it crosses a critical threshold—getting too close to human—our response plunges into revulsion. As firms experiment with anthropomorphic robots with real hair, it remains to be seen whether the valley can be bridged.

At Unitree’s headquarters, the GD01 was displayed hanging from a reinforced steel joist. Wang was unwilling to operate it or even climb inside. “It might not be safe,” he shrugs of his creation, which carries a retail price of $650,000. When TIME’s photographer asked for a nearby promotional background to be relocated, Unitree’s technicians protested that shifting it would interfere with the lidar of the nearby phalanx of G1s practicing that now iconic Spring Festival Gala acrobatic martial-arts display. When the performance finished, those technicians rushed to spray their now sizzling lidar with coolant following that four-minute exertion.

For all Unitree’s lead in the humanoid market, today’s machines remain strangely theatrical: bodies dressed as intelligence, rehearsing a role they have not yet learned to live. “Humanoid robot technology is still in its relatively early stages,” cautions Wang. “It will likely take some time before we see genuine, large-scale deployment. It won’t happen overnight.” Nearby, GD01—part prototype, part prophecy—stands sentinel, as if quietly rebuking his master’s prudence.
